To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetric competition-spatial model is considered, where a single species with homogeneous dispersal patterns expands its population. The influence of asymmetric competition is manifested through faster growth and larger population sizes for resident species. Introducing heterogeneous dispersal leads to a non-local diffusion process, which blends species' locations and influences local abundance. By blending disciplines from ecology and mathematical physics, an analogy between competition-spatial models and Higgs models is developed. Specifically, an analogy between the Green function of the former and an electron wave function in a superconductor is formulated. Blending discrete and continuous models and rescaling time, the competition-spatial model is transformed into a general non-local diffusion model. In a superconducting region, a macroscopic wave function, or the Higgs field, emerges, representing a phase that synchronizes particle motion.
We prove that von Neumann algebras associated with compact regions within abelian quantum double models have infinite type $II$.

Cavity magnomechanics is an emerging field that bridges magnetics and optomechanics to explore magnomechanical entanglement. Our research reveals a method to enhance entanglement through a specific population of a magnetic mode within the cavity magnomechanical setup. By adjusting the population of this mode, we discover an optimal condition that significantly increases the entanglement between the cavity and mechanical elements. The proposed method not only enhances entanglement but also exhibits resilience against variations in system parameters and maintains resilience against disruptions from the magnetic mode's phase or amplitude. Consequently, this strategy may facilitate the efficient generation of entanglement in future magnomechanical systems and help understand its underlying mechanics.

We have obtained one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for color and spin spaces, applicable to all five scenarios allowed by massless QCD theory: $q \to qq'\bar{q}\bar{q}$, $q \to qq' \bar{\nu} \ell$, and $\gamma \to qqq$. 
Our results are expressed as integral expressions involving lower-dimensional splitting coefficients and are also used to describe the $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^2)$ contribution from a $q$ particle splitting into $qq'\bar{q}\bar{q}\bar{\nu}\ell$ in the one-loop triple-collinear color/spin space. 
The derived color and spin coefficients are employed in a parton shower and are expected to be useful in other contexts as well.

A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional case algorithm, has been formulated and applied to one-dimensional local rings, and this concept is currently being used in Singular software implementation. Furthermore, a relevant theorem based on Greenberg's Strong Approximation theorem has also been successfully adapted for use in multiple-dimensional rings.

Ancient sundials were essential timekeeping tools that the classical Islamic civilization used to divide the daily path of the Sun into equal parts and schedule religious activities accordingly. Starting from the 9th century AD, Islamic scholars built upon Ptolemaic astronomy to make a crucial discovery: the varying speed at which the Sun moves through the eastern and western horizons is influenced by the observer's latitude. These scholars then adapted classical sundials to account for this discovery, creating more accurate timekeeping instruments and non-linear scales specifically tailored to their latitude. During the Mongol invasion in the 13th century, many of these sundials lost their purpose and were abandoned. However, they were later revived in the modern era, with researchers today applying similar methodologies to study solar time perception and non-linear scaling in areas where solar time is still used to mark the passage of the seasons.

This paper examines the performance of an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS)-enhanced communication system, where a cellular user equipment (CE) shares resources with a decentralized D2D communication pair. To address data rate limitations for the CE, we incorporate an IRS into the system and design a resource allocation strategy to maximize D2D throughputs. We model the issue as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming problem and, through a series of innovative techniques, transform it into a solvable convex problem. The proposed method, characterized by its ability to utilize reflection, significantly improves the CE's data rate while ensuring its throughput remains within a predetermined disparity from the optimal. Simulations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed scheme in yielding substantial data rate gains for the CE with minimal impact on the D2D pair's throughput.

The surge in telework needs has highlighted the potential benefits of fully
automating and controlling experiments remotely. This work presents the technical
advancements of creating a two-dimensional LDV measurement system using a single-
head laser, controlled through a fully integrated remote networked control system.
This approach is utilized to analyze the response of two-sample assemblies in the
frequency domain, demonstrating its application to characterizing the properties of
a thin film and its underlying substrate material.

The cardinality counting logic, introduced by Durand-Luthereau and Germain in 2019, is capable of capturing the cardinalities of sets defined by binary relations in the extended order logic. Building upon their work, we investigate the expressive power of the counting logic, combined with a single, symmetric, binary relation, denoted as R. Specifically, we focus on counting logic with multiple variables over relation sets that are complementary to each other, along with an R. When considering full-variable sets, we find that any spectrum achievable with multiple variables, given the complement of R (denoted as not-R), can be attained with a single variable, provided we only consider R sets. Furthermore, if the complement of R is also in a single-variable spectrum, then the combined logic of counting and R results in a linear hierarchy. With a finite, transitive, and total ordering, we observe that counting and R yield the same expressiveness as counting alone when dealing with full-variable sets for both R sets and not-R sets. Additionally, if adding an additional binary relation to the standard ordering allows for single-variable definition, then any spectrum achievable with multiple variables, given the ordering and R, can be attained with a single variable, provided we only consider R sets.

The transmission electron microscope (TEM) is capable of imaging by transmitting electrons through a specimen, which scatter and reduce the electron count detected in each pixel, thereby limiting the determination of the electron count to an average value. However, the limitation of the TEM's phase-space resolution is shown to be able to exceed the electron-optical resolution if the electrostatic phase aberration is properly corrected. By doing so, the electron-optical resolution of 0.05 \AA{} is achievable, which results in the formation of a point spread function (PSF) that is nearly isotropic in the momentum-space, while the electron-optical dose limit remains around 10^4 electrons/\AA{}^2, which is largely independent of the pixel size. By measuring the electron count in the image and applying knowledge of the PSF, the electron-count PSF can be determined, which ultimately allows for the reconstruction of the real-space image. Furthermore, the use of a programmable electrostatic phase aberration corrector, such as a programmable electrostatic phase plate (PEP), can enable the TEM to achieve its maximum phase-space resolution. A PEP consisting of a liquid-crystal-coated glass can be designed to reduce Strehl ratio distortions, which typically take around 1000 \AA{} for a 0.2 \AA{} resolution specimen, resulting in the TEM achieving its maximum phase-space resolution.

Drawing inspiration from Feynman's and Deutsch's groundbreaking work, we introduce a theoretical framework that assesses computational capability across diverse physical platforms and complexity scales. This framework is utilized to analyze the fundamental principles of quantum computation. Furthermore, this study serves as a precursor to investigating more universal computation models by examining additional physical mechanisms exemplified throughout the paper.

This study focuses on determining the general equation for calculating the potential positions of an $n$ step random walk in a $d$ dimensional space with a single dimension step of one unit. An explicit expression for the ball of radius $n$ in a $d$ dimensional space is provided, along with the method for computing the population of the surface of this ball, denoted as $B_n$. We employ the representation theory of the symmetric group to establish a formula for $|B_n|$. This population is equal to the sum of certain products of the binomial coefficients.

This research in depth investigates the model of spherically symmetric, asymptotically flat cyclic black holes, derived from quantum gravity principles. We begin by outlining the cyclic black hole model and then delve into analyzing its inherent thermal laws. Building upon this foundation, the study moves on to computing the characteristic frequencies of the black holes' gravitational and electromagnetic wave disturbances, often referred to as quasinormal modes. Notably, frequencies in these quasinormal modes are directly influenced by quantum corrections. Furthermore, the investigation includes calculating the rate of particle radiation emitted during the black Holes' decay process.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material.

Continuous speech that exhibits continuity, emotion, and narrative continuity is referred to as paragraph-level speech synthesis. In this paper, we explore an approach that incorporates speaker state, which encompasses dynamics, emotion, and paragraph-level state, to produce high-quality speech synthesis. This state-based model, trained on continuous speech data, also maintains continuity throughout the speech. The results from the model reveal that incorporating speaker state is a crucial step in generating meaningful speech at the paragraph level. The model is a significant advancement over speech synthesis models that lack state, with notable improvements in CEREAL-10T, a 1000-dimensional speaker state representation, yielding an average relative improvement of 14.6% in CART test sets. The model is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/ayoungjin/ParaTTS-2.

We introduce a novel projection predictive inference method for analyzing non-Gaussian data with model uncertainty and perform relevant variable selection in the framework of finite Gaussian mixture models and latent Dirichlet allocation. By eliminating the need to approximate marginal postérieurs, projection predictive inference facilitates a practical approach to dealing with high-dimensional data sets. Furthermore, our method leverages inherent model sparsity to model variable selection and incorporates a high-dimensional selection indicator vector into the projection pipeline, which is determined through variational inference in the conditional posterior. We evaluate the performance of projection predictive inference in the context of non-Gaussian data regression and community detection in network structures through simulation studies and real-world applications.

Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to model poisoning attacks, where the effectiveness and subtlety of certain techniques are notable. In this study, the impact of these attacks on the robustness of peer networks is investigated, where shared data and collaborative training undermine the effectiveness of the attack. Surprisingly, findings show that the attack succeeds in peer networks at a rate comparable to centralized training and reveals a peer network's robustness advantage in scenarios where the attack compromises a large portion of the training data in a centralized setting. The study further examines various attack and peer network configurations to assess their resilience against attacks and robustness against noise.

Climate change is frequently denied by individuals, with far-reaching implications for the environment and society at large. The dissemination of conspiracy theories may be a driving force behind such denialism, with social media serving as a primary platform. Although research exists exploring conspiracy theories related to climate change, the overall impact conspiracy theories have on individual climate change beliefs remains unclear. In order to address this knowledge gap, this study utilizes a large dataset of Twitter users who engage in conspiracy theory dissemination. By analyzing these users' posts, the study discovers that individuals who actively share conspiracy theories on social media are more likely to engage with anti-climate change content, whereas those who do not share such theories are more likely to share climate change support content. This suggests that sharing conspiracy theories may contribute to the rejection of climate change science.

A study focusing on the production of dark matter in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been carried out using the CMS detector. This analysis involved the examination of collisions resulting in one or more tau leptons and high transverse momentum hadrons in the final state. The data, comprising 35.9 fb^-1 of luminosity, was compared to standard model predictions, revealing a notable excess of events. The investigation led to the establishment of constraints on the mass of the dark matter mediator, encompassing both scalar and pseudoscalar options, in conjunction with existing limits from the ATLAS collaboration. This research provides the most stringent limits to date on the mass of the dark matter mediator for final states containing tau leptons. Moreover, the study includes theoretical bounds on the dark matter cross-section with various new mediators, including the Higgs, Z, and photon.

Given an n-exangulated category with specified properties, we establish that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if it possesses certain duality-based angles. We also determine a specific condition necessary for the presence of Serre duality. Assuming duality exists, we establish a one-to-one correspondence involving a bijection and specific category characteristics.

We develop a treatment effect model that accommodates multiple unordered treatments and various instruments, extending the first difference representation method originally proposed by Haile and Weyl (2017). This framework enables the direct identification of the distribution of treatment outcomes without the need to specify the structural form of the model. Building upon this identification, we define the counterfactual distribution and propose nonparametric tests for various treatment effect parameters, all while minimizing assumptions about the structural model. These new estimators and testable implications generalize the restrictions established by Haile and Weyl (2017), with implications for tests known as the GCS and HW limits, which are then implemented in simulations and an empirical analysis of a clinical trial.

To advance our understanding of matter's various forms, high-energy particle collisions with a wide variety of projectiles are essential.  Although often challenging due to scarcity, particularly in the case of antimatter particles, custom-built antimatter beam production facilities can yield rare particles in the form of beams.  However, the difficulty extends beyond beam production itself; it also lies in the accurate identification of these particles and their secondary products.  While modern tracking systems excel at identifying stable particles, it is not as common to find systems capable of also identifying short-lived particles.  In the fields of subatomic physics and astrophysics, where the study of hypernuclei and rare isotopes could greatly benefit, it has been proposed that the use of a wide-angle muon beam may provide a new, unique tool.  Building upon the ideas developed for the MUonIC experiment, which aimed to examine the proton's magnetic field and its interaction with a 120 MeV/muon beam, further research may be possible.  With the aid of high-performance tracking systems and muon detection systems advanced for the muon tomography industry, which has seen the rise of muon beams as an interesting application thanks to its ease of implementation and potential for wide-angle muography, precise measurements of hypernuclei and rare isotopes may become a reality and lead to significant findings.

Most of a multiple star system's final mass is formed before the first mass ratio is established, but little is known about how accretion occurs in three-star systems during the final stages of formation. The goal of this research is to develop an understanding of the boundary conditions that apply to three-star systems at the end of the classical CHIMPERE model's operation. The goal of the research is to perform numerical simulations of binary star accretion within three-star systems to gain insight into their behavior. By comparing these simulations with analytical models developed using the CHIMPERE code, the researchers have identified areas of agreement and disagreement between the two methods. As a result of the simulations, four key factors were identified as differences between the analytical and binary models: mass accretion rates, binary mass, differential accretion, and mass accretion by the third body. These findings have led to an updated version of the boundary condition model. It has been discovered through the simulations that differential accretion has a greater impact on three-star system dynamics than previously thought and certain rare three-star systems exhibit very large mass variations due to differential accretion. Due to biases in mass accretion simulations, the boundary condition based on the CHIMPERE model overestimates the rate of mass gain by inner binaries and the influence of the outer body's mass on binary evolution. This paper examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, as viable models for understanding the universe on a cosmological scale. We demonstrate that such spacetimes, in intrinsic terms, comprise two de Sitter spaces combined with different orientations. We also establish a reduced canonical form for the metric and identify the associated symmetry group with its associated Schur constant. Additionally, we examine possible extensions of these metrics and discuss how they relate to the FLRW metric at specific points in time.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration techniques enables the proposed model to effectively handle noisy or low-quality input images, while also addressing the challenge of missing data in segmentation tasks. Additionally, the model incorporates both global and local convolution operations to capture long-range contextual links and fine-grained details, respectively. To further enhance the model's performance, we introduce the Top-K Adaptive Gate mechanism, which selectively suppresses irrelevant features and amplifies relevant features for the segmentation task. Extensive experiments on the MS-COCO and KIWI benchmarks demonstrate the proposed method achieves high segmentation accuracy (mIoU of 46.56) for normal images and segmentation accuracy (mIoU of 41.42) for missing labels, outperforming current state-of-the-art models for both scenarios.

Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are extremely bright at various wavelengths, which allows scientists to determine the properties of black holes by analyzing their emitted light. Researchers recently discovered a new way to detect gravitational waves from merging intermediate-mass black holes by observing how their mass and spin affect the agn spectrum. Our study provides the first theoretical predictions for a black hole system that consists of a primary black hole located in a galaxy and a smaller intermediate-mass black hole that is orbiting it. By analyzing the changes in the EM spectrum and gravitational wave frequency, researchers can determine the mass and spin of the black holes, which gives a more accurate estimate of their final mass and spin after they merge. Our findings show the potential for new applications of multi-messenger astronomy, which may help explain the missing components of dark matter and understand the origin of certain gamma-ray bursts.

The development of neuromorphic systems has attracted significant attention due to their unique neural-inspired design. To study and compare these systems, a need arose for a unified testing environment. This environment should be open-source, easy to use, and support various hardware platforms through diverse programming languages. The Spiketrain Emulator Framework (STEF) addresses these requirements by providing a comprehensive framework for simulating neural networks on various hardware platforms, with a focus on comparing the performance of different systems and making them accessible to the research community.

A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated during stellar flares and observed through radio bursts at frequencies between 10^8 and 10^10 Hz. These storms exhibit continuous waves that can change in intensity, frequency, or both, allowing for detailed analysis of particle beam dynamics during stellar flares. We analyzed data from the Radio Spectrograph board on the RHESSI satellite, which captured the evolution of a microflare-associated noise storm between 1999.01.26.06:41:45 and 06:42:15. This storm exhibited two evolution patterns, where one part showed frequency increase followed by intensity decrease, whereas its counterpart exhibited simultaneous intensity and frequency increases. The dynamics behind these patterns suggest two distinct particle beam behaviors, in which one beam undergoes repeated scattering, while the other, unscattered beam interacts with different plasma resonance conditions.

A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that merges an optical grating and a quadrupole magnetic field on a single chip. The grating chip is inserted into a chip-integrated coil to generate the quadrupole magnetic field, which, in conjunction with a 880-nm laser, captures and cools a cloud of approximately 10^5 rubidium atoms, as demonstrated by resonance fluorescence at 795 nm. This integrated MOT architecture offers the advantages of efficiency, miniaturization, and reconfigurability, potentially applicable in various applications such as quantum information processing, photonics, and opto-electronics.

The spherically symmetric fallback rate following a binary star's common envelope phase fails to match observed mass accretion patterns of post-merger black hole high-mass X-ray binaries. To rectify this discrepancy, we replaced spherical symmetry with rotating disk models and compared their fallback patterns to realistic binary mergers. By incorporating angular momentum, mass accretion onto the black hole is significantly diminished and typically decreases by a factor of 10 or more. Although initial post-merger disks would likely be thick, they could thin out to form a thinner configuration over time, potentially restoring the fallback rate to its original value and offering a viable solution to replenish stellar-mass black holes necessary for generating gravitational waves detectable by LIGO and Einstein Telescope.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable and the electromagnetic field was scalar and quantized, considering a moving atom in two dimensions.

A long-term study of massive stars has revealed their presence in a variety of settings, including both dense star clusters and stars field. This has led researchers to investigate whether these entities have formed in isolation or through other means. New observations of O and O type stars with masses greater than 20 solar masses have been conducted using the same methodology as earlier studies but applied to a 22 square degree area of the sky. These stars were found to be distributed uniformly, and further analysis using the GAIA mission's high-precision parallax data confirmed their distances. However, this analysis also highlighted challenges in studying stars of lower mass, as the GAIA mission's limitations became apparent. Ultimately, these results provide a detailed 3D map of local O and O type stars, and in doing so, they confirm that O type stars with masses greater than 20 solar masses can be found in a variety of environments, including dense star clusters and stars field. This finding has implications for our understanding of stellar formation and evolution, and could lead to a significant shift in the prevailing three-channel theory of stellar formation and evolution, which holds that massive stars form only within dense star clusters.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper aging and environmental factors, can become extremely difficult to read. This study proposes an end-to-end handwritten degradation removal framework, consisting of two primary components: the first is a handwritten distortion correction module, and the second is an image enhancement module. The former utilizes a U-shaped architecture to reconstruct the binary document image, whereas the latter combines a binary conversion module and a hand-drawn glyph enhancement module to optimize the overall readability. The proposed framework, which is evaluated on the H-DRR dataset, outperforms existing methods in boosting the readability of both real and synthetic handwritten documents.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly transformed how Information is exchanged, making it essential to establish standardized formats for effective communication. Although technologies like Python's 'pyPDF' can easily convert ID card images to text using the OCR technique, these methods often struggle with non-standard ID card layouts. To address this issue, we propose a new approach that employs a Deep Learning-based segmentation technique to identify and isolate different card card sections, making it adaptable to various card designs.

In vehicular communications, the complex and rapidly changing channel conditions require precise channel estimation, which is limited by the availability of pilots. The limited supply of orthogonal frequency subchannels available for pilots significantly restricts estimation accuracy. The challenge of efficiently designing pilots for channel tracking, given these restrictions, is a crucial issue in this context. The progressive nature of tracking suggests that a small set of pilots may be sufficient for this purpose. However, the optimal pilot allocation strategy remains unclear. The allocation of pilots should consider factors such as the timing of the estimation, the direction of propagation, and the relationship between pilots. The outcomes of this research indicate that non-contiguous pilot allocation tends to be more effective, and the timing and direction of pilots should diverge progressively. The optimization techniques proposed in this study have demonstrated improved performance over traditional methods that allocate pilots evenly. The benefits of these techniques are expected to significantly enhance performance in frequency modulation (FMC) and other related technologies.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered significant interest in the machine learning community. Colorization models based on deep neural networks are particularly effective at this task, although they are often limited by their dependence on extensive manual labeling for training, which is both costly and time-consuming. The problem is compounded by the generally low resolution of the labeled images available, which can lead to overfitting and reduced performance when applied to colorize high-resolution images. To address these challenges, we propose a novel two-stage framework, R2C, consisting of a semi-supervised image restoration step followed by a colorization step. The R2C framework leverages both the colorized and restored images, which improves colorization performance when only partially labeled images are available. The R2C framework is capable of coloring black-and-white photos, while the underlying methods proposed involve a new training technique utilizing color targets as references and incorporating them into the final restored results. The R2C framework achieves notable improvements in colorization performance over existing state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets and provides open-source code for transparency and reproducibility.

We present a novel and efficient numerical scheme for determining Artificial Neural Network weights. Inspired by a classical result in mathematical analysis known as Weierstrass' theorem, our proposed algorithm iteratively refines a polynomial approximation. By translating this approach to neural networks, we demonstrate that its computational complexity can be minimized to nearly linear time, thereby providing a novel neural tangent framework. Building upon this framework, we propose an algorithm capable of achieving a near-optimal approximation error with only a marginally higher sample complexity.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with numerous activities during its first two years of operation.

A novel class of wave phenomena, single and multi-polarized line waves, can form at the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic surfaces, allowing for the creation of precise localized fields perpendicular to the boundary. These line waves exhibit subradiant characteristics and are insensitive to spatial location, making them suitable for integration with various functional components. Furthermore, they exhibit robustness in the presence of irregularities and defects within the boundary system. We demonstrate the theoretical foundation and practical implementation of these line waves in a metasurface design that enables the precise manipulation of localized fields and radiated beams, including polarization conversion and multi-channel communication systems.

One of the most effective approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is learning across multiple interacting agents. This method excels at resolving complex challenges such as communication and knowledge sharing between these agents. This paper explores the complex challenges associated with this approach and the innovative solutions it offers. It primarily concentrates on the communication problems these systems encounter and the potential they possess for shared learning and representation of knowledge. Furthermore, it highlights current research gaps and the promising avenues for further investigation in this field.

A new bias-corrected estimator for the median in a mean-regression model is developed. In conjunction with this development, a corresponding bias-corrected estimator for the quantile regression model is also established. Consistency and asymptotic normality of these estimators are demonstrated. Furthermore, the bias reduction properties of these estimators are confirmed. In terms of performance, the proposed estimators exhibit superior efficiency when compared to their traditional counterparts. These findings were validated through both simulation studies and the analysis of real-world data.

The task of relation extraction is a crucial aspect of natural language understanding, 
which is essential for applications such as question answering and knowledge graph completion. 
However, this process remains challenging due to the difficulty of defining and representing 
ambiguous semantic relationships within sentences. To tackle this issue, researchers employed 
Large Language Models (LLMs) like BERT and XLmR, which have shown significant advancements 
in language and text processing tasks. A novel approach called RelExLLM is introduced, 
which leverages an LLM to recognize and clarify ambiguous relationships between entities. 
This method transforms the relation extraction problem into a classification task and employs 
an LLM to classify the identified relationships. Experimental results on several datasets 
demonstrate that RelExLLM outperforms traditional methods and excels in a wide range of 
relation extraction tasks.

The Analytical Exact Spectral Function Method is used to calculate quarkonium masses in N-dimensional space, taking into account the effects of anisotropy. This approach leads to a higher dissociation temperature than would be expected from isotropic conditions. Furthermore, increasing anisotropy has the effect of increasing the number of quarkonium bound states lost due to cooling.

Our study focused on the magnetic properties of Tb3RuO7, a compound exhibiting D66m symmetry, using neutron diffraction and specific heat measurements. In the parent Tb3RuO7, we observed a complex magnetic arrangement of Ru1 and RU2 moments, indicating a transition from a disordered state to a ordered state at approximately 15 K. The disordered state appears to be influenced by the significant Ru2 thermal magnetism, contrasting with the ordered Tb3RuO7 below 15 K. Doping with Ni in Tb3RuO73NiO with D66m symmetry led to a totally disordered state of Tb and RU moments at room temperature, induced by a slight lattice distortion.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) have achieved significant success in processing images and videos. Despite this success, the reasons behind their effectiveness remain unclear. In our research, we conducted a detailed analysis of the geometric properties of their outputs, which led us to develop a novel representation system. This system uses two separate layers to encode spatial and temporal information separately, which can then be combined to form their product. By doing so, we were able to create a more interpretable representation that separates spatial-temporal information. In our research, we showed that using such representation in models improved their transparency and efficiency without any performance degradation. The code for our system is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/jianfengs/MLP-Representation-Layer.

We introduce a novel, unified approach to covariate-shift adjustment that integrates adaptation and semi-supervised learning. This approach leverages the correlation between target unlabeled data and the source class labels to compensate for the effects of domain adaptation. By utilizing the gradients of both adaptation and adaptation, we can effectively mitigate the impact of domain shift. Experimental results on a real-world dataset demonstrate the superiority of our unified method over existing semi-supervised learning and domain adaptation baselines.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric framework for analyzing deep learning architectures by identifying geometric structures within different models, from convolutional neural networks to recurrent neural networks. We demonstrate that these geometric structures give rise to valuable optimization strategies, such as using Weyl manifolds to derive quantization rules and employing functors to develop truncation methods that maintain performance integrity. Furthermore, our analysis enables a comparison of geometric structures across various models, shedding light on the underlying dynamics of generalization capacity, learning rates, and transfer learning.

We consider a number field K defined by a polynomial f of degree n over the integers, with the defining ring being monogenic. We expand on work by Dade by analyzing an algorithm for identifying generators of primitive ambiguous principal ideals of K at a prime p that splits completely. This analysis also involves examining the analogous issue in p-adic local extensions. Dade's findings show that the identified generators form a subgroup of units modulo p-1, and this result is further refined in our research by proving that, if p does not equal the characteristic of the field and the p-closure of K is p-adic field extension of type T, then the order of this subgroup divides 2(p-1). Dade's findings are specifically applicable when the p-closure of K is a Kummer extension, a cyclotomic extension with a prime conductor, or a totally real Kummer extension, and in these instances, the upper bound on the generator subgroup's order derived from Dade's theorem is precise.

A research framework is introduced to investigate and enhance the performance of deep neural network-based classifiers used in jet substructure tagging techniques. The study focuses on the impact of including additional, manually crafted variables among the input features. To investigate this, a series of tests are conducted on a simplified tagger using various configurations. The research demonstrates that a properly designed set of variables can significantly increase both the accuracy and robustness of a tagger. Furthermore, the study shows that a smaller set of features can be used without compromising accuracy when expert variables are included. These findings have direct implications for developing efficient and interpretable classifiers for real-world taggers.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, and two types of double (intrinsic and extrinsic). Layer group properties such as cosets, subgroups, and orbits were computed symbolically and efficiently. The computation is made possible by the relationship between layer group properties and those of parent space groups. This relationship enables the use of existing software (SLEAP) for computing layer group properties. The input for this computation is the layer group data (LEAP3) generated by solving the coset problem for each layer group type.

Momentum operators are explored on both flat and intrinsically curved manifolds, with a focus on those that are compact in nature. It is demonstrated that the momentum operators defined on these compact manifolds, which can be presented as a quotient of Euclidean space by a crystallographic group, are self-adjoint. Furthermore, an investigation into the Laplacian, particularly its spectrum, is carried out. When a manifold is covered by a solvable, simply-connected Lie group equipped with a left-invariant metric, the Laplacian is also explored, with comparisons drawn to a torus. Finally, the momentum operators are examined within the framework of the Heisenberg group.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant, posing a computational challenge. We present a method to address this issue by applying a local transformation that eliminates the sign problem for any filling level, with the Jacobian cost confined to a localized area. By applying the transformation locally and integrating globally, the remaining sign problem is significantly reduced. Although this approach introduces a residual sign problem, our findings indicate that it remains tractable for larger systems.

A composite Higgs based on a $U(2N_f)/Sp(2N_f)$ setup, with a complex scalar $\phi$, is studied in the context of D-branes in a nontrivial B-field background. The $\phi$ field acts as a complex scalar in a potential that arises naturally from a non-renormalizable operator involving the goldstone matrix $u$. A dual $N=2$ SCFT description, using a supersymmetric quiver in the presence of a B-field, is explored to obtain the effective potential for $u$. The $\phi$'s vacuum expectation value breaks the SCFT conformal symmetry, yielding a potential for the goldstone boson and a massive spectrum. The B-field also modifies the symmetry group and spectrum of the composite state.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, enabling users to traverse farther distances than they can walk and experience objects beyond their reach. Conversely, VPPMs can be detected by users, which disrupts the immersive, wizard-of-Oz state of VR experiences. Perceptual manipulation resistance employs algorithms and techniques to minimize the visibility of these manipulation techniques, typically by directly applying solutions in VR systems, often resulting in limitations in flexibility and the inability to handle multiple manipulation types simultaneously. Our study focuses on the development of a learning-based framework for simultaneously performing and concealing multiple VPPM techniques. This framework can be applied to various VPPMs, such as redirection walking and haptics, and utilizes a virtual agent, an internal simulation, an external feedback simulation, and a multi-agent reinforcement learning system to enable the VPPMs to conceal themselves by predicting user behavior and responses.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent observations by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array have been reanalyzed in a recent paper to study the mass distribution of binary fragments during formation process. The data from the 'Bok4' cluster in the Perseus molecular cloud were utilized in this study. What was found was that the total mass of the core that forms a binary fragment is not directly proportional to the mass of the fragment itself. However, the distribution of the core's remaining mass after fragment formation is significantly dispersed. Subsequently, the mass of the second fragment in a binary system is found to be about one-tenth the mass of the initial fragment. This finding is consistent with the outcome predicted by previous theoretical simulations. It appears that the initial fragment in a binary system is formed first, and then the second fragment is formed later, possibly during a different collapse phase of the protostars that were formed. The mass distribution of singular fragments is similar regardless of the initial core's mass. This suggests that the fragment masses are determined by relatively uniform physical processes that operate on a scale that is about 1000 times the ratio of a protostar's mass to a protons mass divided by a binary system's separation distance in astronomical units. This finding is supported by both theoretical and observational data on a range of binary systems.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel (arKS) kernel-Fast Independent Component Analysis (K-aK-FastICA) method for extracting features from datasets with non-gaussian non-linear (NGN) characteristics, addressing the limitations of previous random data handling techniques. Another approach, based on the m-arcsinh kernel (m-aK), was developed to process random data, but its efficacy was hindered for complex datasets. The proposed m-aK-FastICA method enhances feature extraction for NGN datasets, while the proposed m-aK-FastICA method combines the advantages of both approaches. Experimental results on NGN datasets and a brain imaging dataset demonstrate superior performance of the proposed method, with m-arcsinh kernel size and bandlimit selection validated through cross-validation and an optimal steepest descent algorithm.

This paper builds on existing research into the limitations of certain logical frameworks in determining graph isomorphism. Specifically, it Distinguishes non-isomorphic graphs within the polynomial calculus when degree is bounded and non-isomorphism can be rationalized by a polynomial of polynomial degree. Furthermore, it explores the implications of being able to identify isomorphically distinct graphs in Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) for the bounded-degree extended polynomial calculus.

A subring collection in a ring $R$, sharing the same identity as $R$, is defined as a covering if the sum of its elements equals $R$. The maximum number of subrings needed to fully cover $R$ is designated as the ring's covering number, denoted by $\mu(R)$. In our investigation, we identified the covering number for the integer ring $\mathbb{Z}$, and determined a significant property of rings with a finite covering number, specifically those that are direct products of an odd integer and the set of integers modulo $2^n$.

Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, creating a pressing need to verify its authenticity. The vast amount of information makes it nearly impossible for users to manually verify the accuracy of the claims they encounter. While automated fact-checking services have been established, they primarily rely on human verification and are limited by the information available on their training datasets. This study presents FACTR, a new approach to verify unsupported claims by incorporating the knowledge from news articles and social media, without requiring pre-existing fact verification training data. Building on a semantic matching algorithm, FACTR identifies the most relevant articles and posts, ranks them, and utilizes their content to verify the claims. Evaluation on an English and a German dataset revealed that FACTR surpasses both a baseline and a model trained on existing verified facts in terms of F1 score.

Social media platforms provide real-time information about social and political events such as protests, demonstrations, and riots. However, data from these platforms often includes misinformation and distortion, making it difficult to distinguish genuine news from manipulation. Recent research has shown that while rumors can spread faster than actual events, they can also slow down in the presence of disinformation. In this work, we analyze the relationship between the content of social media data and the temporal dynamics inherent in these data sets. Specifically, we extract features from Twitter data related to the 2020 French parliamentary elections and demonstrate that certain temporal characteristics can be used to effectively distinguish between rumors and factual information. Additionally, we develop new, time-aware features to improve the existing content-based rumor detection methods, which achieve state-of-the-art performance on the RumourEval dataset, prioritizing both precision and recall in the process.

We have developed and documented a software library called skew-spectrum, which helps analyze cosmic structures and estimate fundamental parameters using the weighted skew-spectrum analysis technique. This technique leverages non-linear relationships between the matter distribution and the gravitational potential to distinguish between different parameters, like dark energy, which has different effects on structures of varying sizes. The skew-spectrum, a byproduct of this analysis, provides insights into parameters that affect the skewness of the gravitational potential rather than the matter density itself. The skew-spectrum, therefore, essentially measures the impact of dark energy on the skewness of the matter distribution across various scales. The skew-spectrum, specifically, reveals the interplay between dark energy and matter at various scales by quantifying the ratio of the potential's skewness to the matter density's skewness.

We investigate the integration of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) with the current standard method for achieving robustness against potential attacks. Our analysis reveals that typical adversarial training is prone to over-confident predictions, which significantly weakens the effectiveness of BNN ensembles. In response, we introduce the BNN-based Prediction Uncertainty Calibration Bagnall (PUCB) approach, a new technique for training BNN ensembles that are resilient to potential attacks. Our findings indicate that PUCB outperforms current methods for achieving robustness while maintaining uncertainty predictions. Moreover, PUCB demonstrates robust uncertainty predictions, a critical component for training and deploying reliable and secure AI systems.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused significant disruption, including the complete closure of China. The outbreak also triggered a public information surge, with malicious rumors proliferating on social media and exacerbating public fear. In this study, we analyzed three major social media platforms in China - Baidu Knows, Zhihu, and Weibo - to examine the mechanisms driving the dissemination of rumors. By mapping the relationships and information flow among these platforms, our analysis revealed that their social networks and the public's shared behavior drive rumor propagation. As a result, the spread of rumors on these platforms tends to be asynchronous. Our research provides an understanding of the mechanisms behind rumor diffusion and can inform the development of more effective anti-rumor strategies.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Four methods of dimensionality reduction, including Principal Component Analysis, Independent Component Analysis, Autoencoder, and Sparse Autoencoder, are utilized to compress each pixel of the hyperspectral images into a more manageable feature vector. The compressed vectors are then fed into a classifier to assess classification performance. Using the Indian Pines scene, we compare the classification accuracy of two popular classifiers, KNN and SVM, across varying compression rates. We also examine how the classification accuracy of the original scene compares to the compressed scenes for these classifiers. We found that dimensionality reduction methods can substantially lower the spectral dimension of hyperspectral images without significantly affecting the classification performance. However, we observed that this impact varies based on the dimensionality reduction method and the classifier employed.

Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors, but their immense size makes them impractical due to difficulties in model deployment and inefficient data storage. In an attempt to make them more efficient, researchers introduced the lottery ticket hypothesis, which suggests that a carefully selected subset of network weights can be identified through which the network can be fine-tuned to achieve top-tier performance. Our research introduces an innovative search methodology that leverages the Coarse-to-Fine (CF) strategy to pinpoint such subnetworks. By combining this methodology with the hypothesis, we were able to pinpoint a subnetwork of VIT-B1/16 that, when fine-tuned, matches the performance of the top-ranked models on the ImageNet classification task. Furthermore, we were able to pinpoint subnetworks of ViT-B1/16, Swin-B, and MAE-B/16 that achieve comparable performance to their full networks on the ImageNet classification task.

A novel and efficient computational approach has been developed to predict amide proton chemical shift deviations in proteins, thereby facilitating the determination of secondary structures. This method leverages random forests and combines predictions from multiple protein features, including those calculated with Disfold, a lightweight structure prediction method. The performance of this method is comparable to charge-based methods but with significantly lower computational cost. Furthermore, the success of this approach in predicting secondary structure from Chemical Shift-Based Protein Sequence features has been demonstrated.

The choice of loss function for a deep neural network is a key factor in the learning process, despite extensive loss functions being proposed in the literature, there is no definitive guidance on how to select the most suitable one. This study conducts a thorough evaluation of commonly used loss functions, including cross-entropy, smooth L_1, and cross-entropy, combined with Legendre regularization, to assess their effectiveness on a benchmark dataset.

This review article series begins with a detailed examination of the parquet theory that calculates high-order correlations in a many-body system with strong interactions. Parquet theory is an extension of self-consistent techniques like the G$\Sigma$ method, where additional equations for self-energy components or interaction parts are introduced. These new equations enable the computation of correlations beyond the capabilities of standard self-consistent methods. We will discuss the various approaches for calculating these properties and their historical developments. Additionally, the application of this approach will be limited to zero temperature systems for the purpose of this review.

The process of exciton condensation, where electron-hole pairs spontaneously condense below a critical temperature and spontaneously open a gap in the electron spectrum, has not been experimentally observed in a semimetal-to-excitonic-insulator transition. We present results from a high-pressure study where we observed the continuous transformation from semimetal to excitonic insulator in the excitonic system of single-crystal MoTe$_2$. As the excitonic system underwent transition, we observed the emergence of a gap in the electron spectrum via resistivity measurements. Moreover, we found that transport measurements revealed sliding metallic states on both the electron and hole branches, which were confirmed by terahertz spectroscopy. These findings are consistent with a theoretical model and suggest the possibility of controlling quantum phase transitions through electron-lattice coupling.

In the US, community safety groups utilize an online system to coordinate volunteers who respond to community-reported incidents, which can range from suspicious persons to missing pets. The system a startup developed to collect dispatch information from various communities via text messages has provided us with a unique opportunity to investigate how text messages impact response times and rates. Our analysis of over 300,000 messages and 22,000 reporting periods reveals that messages with a human touch, conveying empathy and a personal connection, lead to significantly higher volunteer response rates compared to neutral messages. Moreover, we found that messages emphasizing individual impacts have the highest response rates, and those with a more urgent tone have lower response rates. These findings can be utilized by senders to increase volunteer responses without seeming pushy.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$, we investigate the superconducting properties of this material in the presence of magnetically-doped layers. Specifically, we model the interaction between magnetically-doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ and a superconducting Bi$_2$Se$_3$ layer through the use of the Fulde-Ferri-Larkin-Occhii (FFLO) effect. By introducing magnetic impurities in the Bi$_2$Se$_3$ layer with a $d_{z^2}$-wave pairing potential, we observe that this results in FFLO superconductivity under an appropriate FFLO momentum. Furthermore, our findings indicate that FFLO critical fields in the FFS are influenced by both the FFLO momentum and the thickness of the superconducting layer. Notably, our analysis reveals the presence of an odd-parity superconducting state under certain conditions of FFLO momentum and thickness, while for other parameter values, we observe a transition to a mixed state of odd and even parities.

Label-efficient active learning samples the most informative instances for
manual annotation. Current methods either estimate a model's prediction certainty
for a single model or draw conclusions from a pool of labeled predictions
for an ensemble. While the former approach is limited to a single model and
potentially suffers from overestimating prediction uncertainty, ensemble-based
methods suffer from a considerable computational overhead due to the need for
multiple model inference per batch. In this work, we propose a novel approach to
active learning that leverages contrastive learning's instance-level
representations for predicting uncertainty in a single model. We show that our
method not only achieves comparable performance to ensemble-based techniques but
also significantly reduces computational overhead by a factor of 30.

To understand how music has evolved over time, individual songs need to be analyzed in detail to capture their unique characteristics. This requires establishing a standardized approach to characterize each song and track any changes from one to the next. This paper focuses on measuring the temporal complexity of songs to detect any underlying patterns or trends. To achieve this, we've developed a database containing nearly 200 years' worth of music, consisting of more than 1.2 million song segments from a variety of artists and genres, covering an extensive frequency range of nearly 10 octaves. This extensive dataset was compiled from 12 million digital files of music extracts. As a case study, we've applied our methodology to measure the evolution of the average complexity of hit pop songs over the past 70 years. Our analysis reveals notable shifts in the overall loudness and temporal structure of these songs. Specifically, the complexity of the songs, as measured by the number of distinct features, has shown an overall increase of about 25% since the 1960s. However, the complexity of the songs, as measured by the Fisher information coefficient, has actually decreased by about 20% over the same period.

A novel class of stochastic processes for partitioning a finite set of $n$ numbers is investigated. In these processes, a probability distribution determines whether a new number will be appended to an existing block or start a new block when it is drawn. This occurs with probabilities $p$ and $1-p$, respectively. The stochastic processes generated vary depending on the nature of this probability distribution. For specific cases, such as when it is a discrete or geometric distribution, exact mathematical characterizations are provided. Additionally, statistical properties and relationships of the blocks and block lengths are characterized, and methods for determining these properties are provided, such as calculating cumulometric functions for block lengths. Furthermore, methods for characterizing dependence in these sequences of block-lengths are presented, such as using the $\ell$-additive dependence coefficient, and asymptotic results for this measure under specific mixing conditions are established.

Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that of proof terms and proof operations. Specifically, it separates the inversion principle into a distinct condition (named I), describing how assumptions are released, and the recovery principle (named R), ensuring that any initial release can be reversed, thereby restricting the introduction of new assumptions. This paper derives and discusses four key metatheoretic results along with related metatheoretic implications: that I and R together constitute a sufficient and necessary condition for both the consistency of the calculus and its termination in terms of reduction. Furthermore, I alone serves as a crucial condition for the calculus's strong consistency.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, yet their widespread adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To mitigate this limitation, we propose a novel, cost-efficient method to learn from human feedback, leveraging the interactions between multiple human agents. We develop a framework for multi-human human feedback reward learning that enables simultaneous interaction of multiple human agents and their preferred policy learning in real-time. This method leverages a human preference model and multiple human agents' continuous stream of comparative feedback. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and its suitability for practical applications through extensive simulations and real-world robotic experiments.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are embodied in "pointed vortex loops," allowing us to concentrate on their corresponding orbits under area-preserving diffeomorphisms on the 2D real plane. The results show that a specific subgroup within these diffeomorphisms preserves the shape of the vortex loop itself, indicating the configuration space is comprised of loops confining a fixed area regardless of the vorticity distribution and any connected points.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that is estimated through techniques like Treatment Effect Estimation (TEP). Two popular approaches, Treatment Effect Transfer Policy (TEP) and nearly orthogonal Average Treatment Effect (nAIPW) estimators, have different implications on policy decisions but both enjoy double robustness and first-order causal pivot properties. Another estimator, AIPW, is double robust but lacks the first-order causal pivot property, leading to a discrepancy in its results compared to nAIPW. When sample sizes are small or TEP and nAIPW exhibit large result differences, choosing between them can be challenging due to their unequal finite-sample biases. We propose a bias-corrected estimator, BC-AIPW, that achieves bias reduction while maintaining double robustness and first-order causal pivot properties. It is formed by taking the observed AIPY and RAIW results and correcting for their individual biases. Through theoretical analysis and simulations, we demonstrate that BC-AIPW results are always more accurate than nAIPW and AIPW in finite samples.

The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current research into lepton flavor universality violations in B-physics, with several ongoing and planned experiments set to significantly enhance data samples from ATLAS and CMS. In the future, upgrades to the LHC are set to be followed by a potential upgrade to the luminosity, with a possible new circular collider designed to increase the center-of-mass energy to 36 TeV significantly better understanding the rarity of $\tau$-related processes. Furthermore, $\tau$ polarisation measurements could greatly improve our ability to identify the $\tau$ and its decay products effectively, significantly enhancing the overall performance of future particle physics facilities.

A new, lightweight atmospheric general circulation model was developed at the Goddard Institute for Space Studies to efficiently investigate the atmospheric response to space weather events. The 3D atmospheric GCM was built upon a well-tested numerical framework, specifically the Spectral Linearized Interpolated Remapped Predictor (SLIPR) model, which has been used to study stratospheric ozone and the general circulation. In this study, the model was configured to simulate the seasonal cycle and the annual temperature and wind cycles in the atmosphere. In addition, a detailed investigation was conducted to assess the model's ability to simulate the formation of weather systems, which is the primary limitation of many climate models. To address this limitation, the model was fine-tuned by increasing vertical resolution, reducing the sea ice bias by adjusting starting conditions and incorporating a sea ice-albedo feedback mechanism, and by reducing the tropical sea surface temperature gradient to a more realistic level. As a result of these adjustments, the SLIPR model with modified initial conditions was able to successfully simulate the formation of weather systems in the atmosphere, which is essential for accurately predicting the atmospheric response to space weather events.

A typical approach to modelling extreme values is the peaks-over-threshold (POT)
method which utilises the generalised Pareto distribution. It has the advantage of
utilising all data recorded below a specific threshold, thus providing more statistical power and
more precise parameter estimates than the return period approach. The estimates obtained are,
however, dependent on the threshold chosen. In an attempt to mitigate this issue, this study
introduces a novel family of threshold-invariant POT model parameters which allow for a more
robust fit of the generalised Pareto distribution. The parameters are defined as the first two
moments of a standardised and centred excess variable and are shown to be sufficient in
situations where the shape parameter is constrained to be greater than -0.5. A fitting method
involving transformation is proposed along with diagnostic checks analogous to Q-Q plots. These
are demonstrated on real data from two hydrological studies.

Off-line reinforcement learning has a major potential impact, but its current capacity is severely constrained due to the difficulty of precisely defining the policy or value function in the presence of complex, high-dimensional data and unknown probability functions. Most existing methods assume the dataset adheres to certain policy constraints or value constraints, ignoring the potential impact of adversary-modified data, which can significantly alter the target value function. This research examines the learning process in the context of modified data and demonstrates the effectiveness of these approaches in the presence of adversary-modified tuples. Our model assumes the adversary modifies a specified fraction of the dataset and can change the rewards, transitions, and policies underlying the dataset. We establish that value-based methods learn a value function with sufficient accuracy and that policy-based methods choose the optimal policy, even in the presence of modified data. Our work differs from adversary-model-free reinforcement learning as it focuses on learning from an entirely pre-collected dataset, while prior research has considered online learning or modified policy-based games. Our results represent the first analysis of the learning process in the context of modified data without any assumptions about the policy or value constraints. Our work also has potential implications for other areas of research, such as robust reinforcement learning and anomaly detection.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with shift types distinct from those they were trained on. These findings underscore a critical limitation in current detection methods and highlight the need for further research on their definition and use.

In recent years, various artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like Brownian machines, they too rely on thermodynamic energy inputs to function. The unique aspect of these motors is their ability to be precisely controlled through the application of specific frequencies and durations of electric currents. A comprehensive understanding of these motors is crucial for realizing their full potential in innovative applications across technology, bio-medical science, and medicine. This review provides a foundational understanding of artificial molecular motors, covering their classification, the underlying physics, and their future prospects. Furthermore, it delves into the concept of molecular gears, a related application that could serve as a molecular version of transplants for treating movement disorders.

Building on a 2017 study, we examine various approaches to interpreting transducers when they involve multiple possible translations for the same input, based on different states. We analyze how these approaches relate to each other and explore their implications regarding specific problems such as inclusion, emptiness, and membership. Notably, we discovered that while origin transducers can recognize non-deterministic context-free languages, deciding transducer emptility is a task that is undecidable. Conversely, we found that under classical interpretation rules, both origin and classical notions are equivalent, and undecidability issues such as inclusion arise in relation to closure under complement.

The concept of $f$-Convolution generalizes the standard convolution operation by introducing a group $f \colon D \to \mathcal{G}_{\text{Ab}}$ and a new operation $\star_f$ on two functions $A, B \colon D \to \mathcal{G}_{\text{Ab}}$. By applying the naive computation method, the $f$-Convolution can be calculated in $\mathcal{O}(|D|^2 \cdot \textrm{cost}_f)$ time, where $\textrm{cost}_f$ represents the cost of performing a single $f$-Convolution coefficient calculation. In this study, we explore the possibilities of speeding up the computation and establish a lower bound of $\Omega(|D|^{\frac{2}{\omega'(\mathcal{H}_f)+1)})$ for any $f$-Convolution computation, where $\omega'$ is a modified version of the matrix multiplication exponent and $\mathcal{H}_f$ is a hypothesis group associated with $f$. In addition, for a specific class of structure-rigid groups $\mathcal{GR}_{\text{Ab}}$, we established an upper limit of $\mathcal{O}(|D|^{\frac{\omega'(2,|G_{\mathcal{H}_f}^{*f}})+2}{\omega'(\mathcal{H}_f)+1)})$

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1992 marked a major achievement for astronomical retrievals. Over 25 years later, multiple model analyses have investigated its atmospheric composition, yet modern spectroscopic model fits for GJ 229B remain unresolved. Our study reveals two distinct solutions that accurately reproduce the observed spectrum: $M_{\rm est}=0.045\,M_{\odot}$ and $T_{\rm eff}=2500\,{\rm K}$ as well as $M_{\rm est}=0.025\,M_{\odot}$ and $T_{\rm eff}=2200\,{\rm K}$. Our results suggest that GJ 229B's atmospheric models may be missing key physical or chemical processes.

To search for the potential existence of the $c\bar{c}ss$-exotic state $D^-\_sD^0\bar{K}^0$, its production likelihood was analyzed using the missing-mass technique on data collected from $\psi(3686)$ decays by the BESIII experiment. The experimental conditions involved a cross-section upper limit of $4.7 \times 10^{-4} \text{ pb}$ at 90% confidence level, assuming no significant background signals and at the 3$\sigma$ confidence level, which corresponds to the current search for an exotically produced state. Based on the findings, the possible existence of the $c\bar{c}ss$-exotic state below 2 GeV remains uncertain.

A crucial goal of the LHCb experiment is to measure the $|\phi_s|$ mixing-induced $C\!P$-violating phase and the lifetime difference of the $B^0_s$ and $B^0$ mesons. Our approach involves combining two independent measurements of $\phi_s$ from decay modes $B^0_s\to J/\psi K^0$ and $B^0_s\to \mu^+\mu^-$, which yield separate estimates of the branching fraction and decay-time difference. We have also developed an enhanced analysis of the $\mu^+\mu^-$ decay, incorporating improved vertexing and a revised background analysis based on the most significant dimuon contributions.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately influenced by the complex interplay of airflow patterns, ventilation methods, air circulation, and occupancy levels. This study employs a theoretical model to analyze how viruses spread through aerosols in a vehicle. It examines the transportation of these aerosols using the advection-diffusion equation and investigates the dynamic behavior of this system. This model reveals that key factors such as occupancy, window openings, and fan speed significantly impact the spread of infectious aerosols, highlighting their importance in understanding the dynamics of virus transmission. This model offers a valuable tool to estimate the probability of virus-laden aerosol transport and is further developed to create a practical application. This decision support system helps vehicle operators assess their exposure to infectious aerosols and make informed decisions about vent settings to mitigate transmission risks. It represents a valuable public health resource in helping transport operators make informed choices to prioritize passenger and crew well-being.

This study has conducted large-scale shell-model computations for $\beta^-$ and $\beta^+$ $\Delta$-decisions with $np$ and $np$ shell Model spaces, covering both the $f_{7/2}$ and the $f_{5/2}$ $f_{3/2}$ $f_{2/2}$ shell models. We have calculated $\beta^-$ and $\beta^+$ decay properties and have focused our research on isobaric multiplet members. Experimental data have been used to determine half-lives and decay branching ratios. Our calculations have revealed a strong correlation between the transition probabilities of $\beta^-$ and $\beta^+$ decays and the energy differences between the initial and final states in the corresponding parent and daughter nuclei. We have examined unique first-forbidden $\beta^-$ and $\beta^+$ transitions in specific isobaric multiplets, including $A=67$, $A=68$, $A=71$, and $A=78$. Our findings have been compared with other theoretical models, including shell-model calculations, and have been found to have reasonable agreements with those results.

Double-sided auctions are a fundamental concept in economic theory used to analyze various financial markets. In recent years, researchers have extended this concept to securities lending markets and found that it offers more than just a theoretical framework. The application of double-sided auctions in securities lending results in significant benefits, including improved price discovery, reduced basis risk, and enhanced market liquidity. To facilitate this, a double-sided auction platform has been developed using the Ethereum blockchain technology. The platform enables market participants to submit multi-quantity buy and sell orders for securities, facilitating efficient matching and execution of trades. A non-custodial and transparent platform is crucial for securities lending to maintain the integrity and security of the process. We have designed and implemented a double-sided auction platform using the Ethereum blockchain, which serves as an efficient and transparent ledger for the industry.

We utilized heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we derived upper limits on their corresponding coupling values. Our research further included an analysis of the $F$-wave light pseudoscalar and vector bottom mesons, with masses computed using the same method.

Michal Szabados initially proposed a theory in his doctoral dissertation. In this current paper, the idea of periodic lines has been explored in a different context by another researcher. Specifically, periodic lines were defined within the set of periodic configurations. Demonstration of the existence of nonexpansive lines among periodic configurations has been confirmed through a different approach. Furthermore, the number of periodic lines in various nonexpansive directions has been determined in this research. An important finding is that the number of periodic lines can be made arbitrarily large. To achieve this, a method is provided to construct lattices that contain periodic configurations with an unlimited number of periodic lines. Additionally, the research shows that these constructed configurations have the property of being locally isomorphic to that of the SOST lattice, which is known to have a different count of periodic lines. This discovery raises a significant question: does the set of periodic configurations truly encompass all configurations that have a different property of being locally isomorphic to that of a specific model configuration?
