By allowing users to select multiple relay vehicles, I-SCFRS outperforms existing schemes in terms of sum-rate through a substantial margin.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an encyclopedic resource, 
yet only 0.6% of its articles are currently considered of high quality. 
Our study delves into the characteristics of high-quality articles 
across the 282 languages supported by the Wikipedia International. 
By examining nearly 2 million articles, we utilize machine learning 
to assess quality based on key attributes including article length, 
number of revisions, and the number of unique article contributors. 
The analysis identifies clear patterns linking high-quality articles 
to larger languages such as English and German, but reveals these 
qualities fall short in smaller languages like Indonesian and Korean. 
Notably, our findings contradict the prevalent assumption that articles 
written by a limited number of contributors are of superior quality. 
Instead, we observe that articles contributed to by a diverse range of 
individuals are more likely to be of high quality.

Knowledge distillation is a crucial technique for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-performance network. Traditionally, this involves teaching the model to replicate the 'predictions' of the original network, measured by the distance between sample inputs and output logits. A novel approach focuses on distinguishing between similar inputs, which requires the model to effectively separate similar samples in the feature space. This new method ensures the model preserves the similarity relationships of the original network, rather than simply matching its predictions. We show that this new approach leads to better generalization and achieves better performance on the imageNet benchmark with less overfitting.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ data set collected by the LHCb experiment at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. The branching fractions for these decays were measured at $4.2\cdot 10^{-5}$ and $1.7\cdot 10^{-5}$, respectively.

The torus $T^d$ plays a fundamental role in string theory as the simplest example of topological T-duality. Building upon this, researchers have since explored topological T-duality on more general spaces such as bundles and other manifolds. In our study, we've successfully derived the local expression of topological T-duality for a broad class of spaces known as solvmanifolds, specifically those that are nearly abelian in nature. Our approach employs the method of twisted K-theory to establish this duality, with the twisting resulting from a four-form generated by the natural symplectic form on the torus factor. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that our framework can be employed to investigate topological T-duality within the context of two-torus bundles. Our work also encompasses a detailed analysis of twisted K-theory for the case when the underlying space is compact and diffeomorphism-invariant.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert knowledge. However, in practical applications, expert demonstrations are often scarce due to the expense and complexity of obtaining them. To overcome this limitation, this research introduces a novel, unsupervised imitation learning framework, centered on the principle of unsupervised peer learning. By employing unsupervised peer learning, agents can infer demonstration trajectories from agents without explicit supervision. To tackle the challenges associated with imitation, such as the copy signal problem and the degradation of copy signals over time, the proposed framework integrates the existing knowledge of both the agent and the demonstrator. As a result, the proposed framework enables effective policy acquisition even in the absence of supervised demonstrations. Experimental findings on both synthetic and real-world tasks reveal that the proposed framework outperforms existing baseline methods.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average for decoding convolutional and PAC codes without an iterative process. Our proposed function outperforms previously suggested functions, such as the ARA, particularly for PAC codes which offer higher error-correction capabilities at the cost of increased decoding complexity. By tailoring the function to PAC codes, we achieve a performance gain and make soft-output Viterbi decoding (SVD) more efficient than previously possible.

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions of multiple hands and distinguishing between them in depth images. To tackle this challenge, we introduce the Hand CANonicalization LIne (HCanLin) system, which combines a customized canonicalization module with an extension of the Kalman filter. The system estimates the scale, rotation, and joint configurations of each hand from its canonical form in the image space. To track multiple hands and identify which ones are in view, we introduce a novel state representation and an innovative reassociation strategy. The effectiveness of HCanLin is demonstrated by extensive experiments on the challenging Handsv2 dataset, even when hands are close together or occluded. Additionally, the system's effectiveness is verified through experiments on the MR-Jaib dataset for reading the letter R with multiple hands.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on a single static and eye-tracking-based dynamic intrinsic calibration. The proposed system avoids the reliance on fiducial markers like the V-Point, which are typically employed. It utilizes a computer vision algorithm to detect a user's face and a deep learning-based face landmark detector to automatically identify facial features. Building on a recent publication, a revised surface normal estimation method enhances the robustness of our approach. The associated tracking system maintains a persistent visual and eye-motion-based extrinsic calibration, which is achieved without the use of any physical markers. Additionally, our proposed system boasts an improved efficiency due to its simplified calibration and tracking architecture.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing standard methods of analysis in terms of correctness and efficiency.

The capability of neutrino detectors like IceCube and Super-Kamiokande to identify the dark matter signal within neutron stars hinges on the ability of neutrons to detect the energy released by the annihilation of dark matter particles. While earlier studies focused on neutrino production through self-annihilating dark matter, recent investigations have expanded to include the potential of Majorana fermions forming bound states before annihilating. In a neutron star's dense core, these bound states are predicted to annihilate and produce an additional neutrino signal. We examine neutrino production on its own, disregarding the emission that occurs as a result of the dark matter's decay or the decay of residual bound states. By simulating the core of a neutron star, we calculate the annihilation rates and the resulting neutrino flux. Our analysis indicates that the dominant reactions involve the annihilation of the bound state with a Majorana fermin, leading to a diverse range of particles. The most notable outcomes are an enhanced neutrino signal, which could be 1-2 orders of magnitude higher than that produced by the direct annihilation of the dark matter, as well as a shift in the energy spectrum towards the high-energy end. The detector's sensitivity in three plausible neutron star core scenarios is also evaluated.

The ongoing and most significant constraint on the $\Lambda$CDM model is the tension between the local measurement of the Hubble constant and the Planck satellite's prediction of the standard cosmological model. To investigate the potential of cosmography using cosmclid in a future survey like LSST, the software cosmoclid has been developed and implemented in a mock survey. This mock survey is based on a cosmological background that incorporates two significant biases: a residual multiplicative shear bias of $5 \times 10^{-4}$, a non-flat universe, a additive shear bias of approximately $5 \times 10^{-4}$, a non-Standard value of Omega-m, a late-time dark-energy equation of state that varies over time. The co-analysis of cosmclid's results with other cosmological probes has been used to determine the feasibility of using cosmclid as a tomographic probe for future surveys. This is achieved by correcting for the additive shear bias and by mitigating the effects of systematic errors, specifically by reducing the residual multiplicative shear bias to the level of $10^{-5}$. This level of precision has been confirmed through multiple analyses, including a co-analysis with other cosmological probes which has shown cosmclid to be a valuable cosmological probe that could be used in conjunction with other data to determine the Hubble constant.

A notable result by Kesten demonstrates that, given an irrational number alpha and a collection of real numbers a_n, the parity of the count of set elements n in the interval [0,T] that satisfy floor(n*alpha) equaling a_n for specified values of a_n will exhibit certain patterns as T approaches infinity. Our investigation builds upon Kesten's finding and considers instances where the given collections follow specific, time-dependent statistical states, with an emphasis on scenarios in which the given counts follow these states for all time and lead to evenly distributed parity frequencies. We find that such scenarios occur when the underlying number system has an infinite continued fraction and a related number theoretic function exhibits self-similar statistical states, and provide instances where the parity frequencies fail to converge. This research connects to higher-dimensional cases, offering explicit examples for d-dimensional scenarios, especially for numbers alpha that exhibit non-unique ergodic ground states.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a multi-dimensional spin system made up of a series of two-dimensional CePmO_7 Heisenberg layers that are weakly coupled through a helical compound. These correlations emerge when the dimension of the helical component is reduced to two dimensions. Research into the spin correlation properties of these systems has been conducted using neutron scattering and is the first to be carried out in a two-dimensional multi-dimensional Heisenberg system with a well-known parameter.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a dark matter particle to the standard model results in the AU MSM (AUMSM) model, a variation of the ADDL (See-Saw) model. In a scenario where the AUMSM model's axion-like particle and a heavy vector-like lepton (specifically $E_3$ and $N_X$) contribute to both neutrino oscillations and dark matter, we find a viable framework. Our research focuses on examining the parameter space consistent with the fermionic DM direct detection experiments within this model. We discover that there are two mechanisms for mass generation in the $a\mu$-based DM model, each with distinct implications for the particle's interaction with nuclei. Additionally, we investigate the correlation between the fermionic DM model parameters and the vector-like lepton's constraints from future $e^+e^-$ colliders. We further analyze the correlation between the fDM parameter space and a previous LHC search for $E_3$ and $N_X$, demonstrating a high level of consistency with other experimental constraints on the model parameters.

This study optimizes existing estimates for the accuracy of state tomography when performing measurements on copies of the magic state, revealing an improved upper limit on stabilizer rank, which is a key measure of non-linearity in quantum states. By applying a unique decomposition of non-stabilizer states into stabilizer states, the research provides precise values for stabilizer rank and derives enhanced bounds for fidelity estimation errors, outdoing prior research by a significant margin. Furthermore, the researchers develop an exact state reconstruction algorithm for states consisting solely of magic gates, achieving a level of precision that was unattainable before.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios: 
when the Hubble parameter's volume defines the energy density's boundary, and when the energy density's boundary defines the universe's volume. Numerous graphical representations are created to analyze the model. 
We investigate the relationship between energy density and its fractional behavior. 
When the universe is described by the Hubble parameter, we find that for any value of the Tsallis parameter greater than one, the model fails to represent a real universe. 
Conversely, when the energy density describes the universe, we discover multiple real universe solutions, with the model transitioning from an accelerated to decelerated phase for both scenarios. 
We also calculate two key cosmological parameters to describe dark energy state equations, and find that for any value of the Tsallis parameter greater than one, solutions do not describe a real universe. 
When the energy density describes the universe, we find that for values less than one, solutions do not describe a real universe. 
Subsequently, we calculate the sound speed of the model, and find it remains positive, thus avoiding potential instabilities. 
Finally, this work examines two acceleration scenarios, and we determine the values of key cosmological parameters for both solutions.

Between January 2018 and December 2020, the LAMOST conducted a 3000-square degree survey in the southern celestial hemisphere, covering a wide range of galactic longitudes (300-360 degrees) at the latitude of at least -10 degrees. This project involved obtaining approximately 1,100,000 low-resolution spectra, with the remaining spectra broken down into four categories according to data quality. Specifically, 50.44% of the spectra met high standards, meeting a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 10, whereas 21.18% met moderate standards, having a signal-to-noise ratio between 5 and 10 within an 800 Angstrom window centered at 5100 Angstroms. Data from pilot runs are presented in Zhang et al. (2021), and the latest results are reported here. Future data releases are already planned, with data expected to be released in 2022.

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs to replace or supplement current TRNGs due to their ability to leverage SRAM's inherent variability in transition times for randomness generation. TRNMG-SRAM, an SRAM-based TRNG, is developed to leverage the memory characteristics variability for more effective randomness extraction. By combining the transition times of read operations and SRAM cell current drive variability, TRNMG-SRAM achieves higher entropy at a lower cost, utilizing two read operations and one comparison for its PRNG design. TRNMG-SRAM demonstrates a 4.12x and 1.71x improvement in throughput over other SRAM-based TRNGs, as well as passing all industry-standard and a new entropy-based FIPS 140-2 and NIST standards.

A pioneering electronic device with the capability to store information, called a memristor, has been studied through computer simulations of the device's response to electrical stimuli. We investigated the behavior of molecular assemblies, consisting of inorganic molecules and ionic liquid, in resistive switching memory applications of sub-10 nm size. These assemblies exhibit a high density of information and the capacity to store information outside the memory's physical boundaries. The simulations revealed that these devices can achieve an extremely high density of information, surpassing $10^7$ bits per square nanometer, and can maintain data integrity through self-repairing mechanisms. Furthermore, we discovered that these devices can utilize their small size as an advantage to distinguish between various amounts of information, effectively utilizing quantum effects to their benefit.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing multi-loop scattering amplitudes in QCD. This method is rooted in Feynman parameters and cuts the loops in the loop energy. A key advantage of LTD is that it identifies regions of the loop energy where the integrand becomes singular. By exploiting these regions, the integrand can be simplified and its evaluation reduced to cutting the loops in the loop energy. As a result, the computation of multi-loop amplitudes becomes more efficient. However, the approach still faces a significant challenge in that it requires a reliable algorithm for determining these regions, which remains to be fully developed. Until this issue is resolved, the application of LTD remains limited to the computation of two-loop amplitudes.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by classical mathematicians like Weyl and Titchmarsh.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The occurrence of phase transitions in optomechanical systems undergoing steady-state transitions, and their amplification through laser noise and atomic flux noise, and their magnification through quantum metric fluctuations, and a generalization of these phenomena via $q$-deformation, and the effects of $q$-deformation on phase transitions and quantum amplification are examined. $q$-deformation impacts the critical point, restoring symmetry and reverting the system to its $q \rightarrow 1$-limited case with quantum amplification properties.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies with distinct shapes, exhibited distinct resonance and absorption characteristics. Building upon this work, I further investigated the scissors states' scattering behavior, assuming that the particles on the rotors' periphery interact with external particles through a direct central mechanism, again assuming the Two-Rotors Model. As expected, bodies with an R-negative configuration displayed a characteristic preference for backward direction in scattering, a feature that is also observed in hadrons. Furthermore, it was found that in both scattering and collision processes, the R-negative scissors states exhibit a characteristic energy tendency to be scattered at low angles or collided centrally.

A phenomenon in which very thin films of metallic transition-metal oxides lose their insulating behavior and become conductive is known as the threshold of delocalization. In this study, we investigate the threshold of delocalization by examining the optical transmission and interband transitions in a material called $\mathrm{V_2O_3}$ with different thicknesses and doping levels. Our results show that the energy at which this conductive transition occurs increases significantly when the film becomes thinner. The delocalization transition is driven by an interband charge transfer that is sensitive to the immediate surroundings, and we observe that the energy behavior at this transition can be linked to the changes in the material's insulating state. Furthermore, we investigate how the material's charge carriers interact with each other and determine that the interactions are comparable in both the metallic and insulating phases, and that the threshold of delocalization is essentially a delicate balance between the energy costs and gains that characterize the material's electronic structure.

The notion of diffusion can be expanded upon by considering "anomalous" diffusion, characterized by a non-exponential distribution of displacements over time. This type of diffusion often arises in systems where trapping mechanisms are present. Researchers have developed an "unscreened" or pure form of anomalous diffusion to better understand these dynamics. By taking into account trapping mechanisms within an infinite system, the traditional description of diffusion, based on the Maxwell distribution, is now insufficient. Researchers propose an adjusted, screened version of the anomalous diffusion model to be applicable in the context of Poisson distribution. This new approach accounts for a non-exponential distribution of trapping times, ultimately leading to the creation of an anomalous Maxwell distribution. This screened anomalous diffusion is applicable in various low-dimensional systems where a critical phenomenon is influenced by an essential free boundary condition. One notable example is the critical behavior of percolation in two-dimensional systems.

In cryptocurrency ecosystems, networks of digital assets and platforms interact dynamically, generating complex, multivariate time series data that can be analyzed using advanced statistical methods. This study leverages the cryptocurrency networks from November 2020 to July 2021 to examine the relationships between tokens within these networks, specifically among stable coins, major tokens, and exchange tokens. By applying unique statistical measures to capture both instantaneous and persistent token relationships, we can assess the resilience of cryptocurrency markets and how these markets adapt in response to significant real-world events. Our initial findings indicate that the behavior of stable coins is heavily influenced by major tokens, in contrast to exchange tokens, whose dependencies on multiple token categories fluctuate. Moreover, the role of stable coins as a store of value is particularly vital during periods of heightened volatility and lasting only for major tokens during turbulent times.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial process that contributes to the creation of cloud condensation nuclei (CCN), the essential foundation for clouds to develop. The capacity of these nuclei to hold condensing water molecules directly impacts the amount of liquid water present in clouds. The most effective way to study the effects of CCN on the climate and cloud behavior is through the observation of their response to different chemical compositions and the presence of gas-phase species in the atmosphere. The latest advancements in the technology for detecting sub-CCN sized particles have enabled researchers to experiment with the response of these particles to the presence of various gas-phase species and the initial composition of the nucleus. The model that we suggest in this study uses the initial composition of the nucleus as a parameter to evaluate the effect of gas-phase species on the final size of the nucleus without having to rely on the detailed internal structure of the nucleus. We compare our model's predictions to the outcomes of numerical simulations of nanoparticles formed from water and sulfuric acid, and the results show a strong agreement with the results of these simulations.

We establish a one-to-one correspondence between compact perception pairs and a specific type of measurement spaces called totally bounded. Furthermore, we develop one method for constructing compact perception pairs and examine some properties of these pairs, including criteria for when they are equivalent. This research deepens our understanding of optimal sensing design.

The way solids respond to gravitational variations on a quantum level remains largely unexplored. In this study, researchers investigated the impact of gravitational potential fluctuations, denoted by delta-g, on the flow of energy and transport properties in solids. They found that the gravitational potential delta-g induces energy currents flowing in multiple dimensions and can lead to the flow of heat when combined with thermal energy. These effects are anticipated to be detectable in ultra-sensitive micro-cantilever systems used to measure the fundamental limit of gravitational constants. Additionally, delta-g may be utilized as a precise tuning mechanism for studying quantum phase transitions and manipulating quantum states.

In various machine learning domains, there's a growing emphasis on model simplicity, where it's understood that more complex models may lead to subpar performance. Within deep learning, there's a growing need for a clear definition of model complexity, particularly since the trend has been dominated by complex models. This paper explores the concept of geometric model complexity, defined by a dual representation of function families as a combination of their mapping properties and the submanifolds they're constructed from. By applying this definition to deep learning models, we're aiming to provide a universal metric for model complexity, enabling a comparative analysis. Our analysis of the impact of network architecture on geometric model complexity is supported by empirical evidence, demonstrating that increasing the depth of a network results in more complex models.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay scoring has been long explored using statistical and deep learning methods. Despite a recent surge in interest due to the availability of large pre-trained language models, such as BERT and RoBERTa, with excellent linguistic capabilities, there have been limited attempts in this field. Our analysis revealed that the best-scoring models from earlier decades still dominate and set a benchmark that even the most advanced recent approaches, employing neural networks and deep learning, struggle to match. To address this challenge, we conducted a comprehensive study on the impact of pre-trained language models on automated essay scoring. By integrating BERT and RoBERTa with traditional linear models, such as logistic regression and support vector machines, we achieved remarkable results that significantly outperform and surpass even the most advanced recent approaches. Our best model, combining BERT with a support vector machine, demonstrated a 12% enhancement over the previously best-scoring model and was subsequently dereferenced. We have made our dataset and pre-trained models accessible to the research community on GitHub.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples.

A higher education degree is often seen as a vital factor in social mobility. 
There is more mobility between generations when the parents who have a degree go 
on to have children who are able to achieve the same degree. In a comparative 
study, there is greater intergenerational mobility in the United States for the 
bachelor's degree. A number of factors could be responsible for the difference. 
One of those factors could be the relative value of a degree. When the proportion 
of individuals who have a degree increases and opportunities become more 
competitive, there could be a corresponding decrease in intergenerational 
mobility. A number of studies have looked at this hypothesis and used the 
individuals who are at the margin between obtaining a degree or not. A number 
of systems are in place. In the United States, there is a degree systems that 
is largely uniform, but in the UK, there are degrees systems that are both 
larger and more complex. In France, there are degrees systems that are both 
larger and more complex, but there are individuals who are confused about the 
value of a degree, which could lead to bias in the results of the studies. A 
study in France aims to overcome this issue. A study focuses on the individual 
who has a degree, but does not go on to get a master's degree, which is treated 
as a reference group. A study uses the individual's performance in the entrance 
exam and their background

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in a delegated manner. Our Delegated RingCT method maintains the original's security, but at the cost of increased logic complexity and lower performance. To balance this, we propose a revised version of Delegated RingCT that significantly simplifies its process and markedly enhances its efficiency.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial observation of three massive gauge bosons being produced simultaneously in high-energy proton-proton collisions at the LHC, using a 13 TeV data set collected by the ATLAS experiment. These collisions, which yielded an integrated luminosity of 130 fb$^{-1}$, resulted in the standard model predictions for diboson and triboson processes being well supported by the experimental data. When considering all relevant final states, the observed standard model agreement reached a significance of 3.1σ, whereas the predicted significance for new physics contributions was 2.4σ. The comparison between experimental data and standard model predictions also included a quantification of theoretical uncertainties for diboson and triboson processes.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on English-centric
annotation guidelines and tools, which are often unsuitable for Hebrew due to its
distinct linguistic characteristics. This study evaluates the suitability of
established NLP tasks for Hebrew and offers proposed tasks with tailored
annotation guidelines specifically designed for the language. These tasks
include pre-trained Hebrew language models, and experiments are conducted to
determine the effectiveness of these models on the new tasks. The study
finds that foundation models outperform traditional NLP tasks in most
scenarios, with room for improvement in other cases. A notable challenge
remains the limited availability of a fully annotated gold-standard dataset
for Hebrew NLP.

We maintain in L_p for any set of functions containing up to m elements, where its maximal value can be represented through an almost-isometric reduction of its dimension, maintaining a precision of ε while reducing the function count to its log base 2 of p or p if p is greater than 4. Furthermore, in the case where p exceeds 4, this representation can be achieved at a function count of the order $\tilde{O}(p^{1/4}\sqrt{p}\sqrt{m}\epsilon^2)$, whereas for p three or less, this count reduces to $\tilde{O}(p\sqrt{m}\epsilon^2)$. Our research also establishes corresponding lower bounds for isometric dimension reduction when the function set is randomly chosen, where for p three or less, the function count cannot be reduced below $\tilde{\Omega}(pm\epsilon^2)$, and for p greater than three, the function count cannot be reduced below $\tilde{\Omega}(p^{3/2}m\epsilon^2)$.

In recent years, deep learning has achieved remarkable success across a broad range of applications. Nevertheless, the vulnerability of deep neural networks to data scarcity and the exacerbation of the trade-off between forgetting past data and acquiring new knowledge hampers their further advancement. To address these limitations, researchers from diverse fields collaborated to develop efficient continual learning techniques that overcome the problem of catastrophic forgetting in artificial neural networks. This work presents an overview of the most recent advances in continual learning for deep neural networks, including the A-weighted Hebbian learning approach and novel methods leveraging generative models and retraining techniques, as well as an exploration of A-weighted forgetting and regularization methods and their potential implications for related problems.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume uniform and uncorrelated connections between variable and check nodes to predict thresholds for successful decoding. In this research, I conduct an in-depth theoretical study to analyze the impact of correlations between degrees of variable nodes and check nodes in LDPC ensembles. I develop a new method to calculate the thresholds for belief propagation (BP) and LDPC codes with degree distributions assigned to specific positions. Ensembles with this property can serve as foundational building blocks to construct more complex, correlated LDPC ensembles. Ensembles with this property are not limited by a single fixed threshold but comprise a broader class, which, in certain situations, yields significantly higher thresholds than the standard BP threshold. Notable examples include ensembles formed from combinations of degrees of variable nodes and check nodes. Furthermore, I investigate how correlations between degrees of variable nodes and check nodes affect LDPC codes' ability to correct erasures and demonstrate that correlations between degrees of variable nodes can result in substantial coding gains.

An advanced MPC-based method, known as the safety filter, has been proposed to ensure the safe operation of predictive controllers despite their inherently open-loop nature. This safety filter acts as a safeguard, allowing safe adjustments to the optimal solutions found by the primary MPC. A variation of this safety filter, the stochastic safety filter, has recently been developed to incorporate probabilistic constraints and allow a greater degree of flexibility in its formulation. This paper introduces an improved version of the stochastic safety filter that offers greater permissiveness and computational efficiency compared to existing formulations. Furthermore, the proposed safety filter can be combined with primary MPC designs that have limited or no support for handling disturbances and modeling errors, such as model predictive controllers that rely on safety filters as a means of handling such issues.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to attacks exploiting device defects. Theoretical solutions, such as measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD, have been proposed to mitigate this issue, and our team previously achieved the world's first field demonstration of MDI-QKD. However, due to the non-ideal characteristics of quantum channel and devices, MDI-QKD is not as secure or efficient as ideal theory suggests. To improve the reliability and performance of MDI-QKD, our team successfully developed the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) postprocessing protocol, which accurately models real-world device defects and significantly enhances its security and efficiency. Notably, using this MLE protocol, we increased the key generation rate by as much as 2.8 times without compromising security, outperforming previous records and ideal MLE-based QKD in certain scenarios.

Recent breakthroughs in large language models (LLMs), particularly in in-context learning (ICL), have been achieved through the strategic use of numerous context examples. Although prior studies have examined ICL from various perspectives, such as from a theoric and computational lens, the effect of pretraining corpus sources on ICL remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the relationship between an ICL model's performance and the source of its pretraining data source. We examine how different corpus source mixtures influence IML's performance on a diverse set of 11 benchmarks, across 14 models, encompassing both open-source and proprietary models. The findings indicate that, contrary to expectation, most corpus source mixtures do not yield improved IML performance and some even result in decreased performance. Moreover, our analysis reveals that varying the ICL model's source has a more substantial impact on ICL performance than the model itself. These results offer significant insights and guidance for developing more effective ICL strategies. The study's code and data are available at https://github.com/uyyabas/EffectOfCorpusSourceOnICL

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nuclear galaxies, but this process is not entirely dependent on such observations. The effects of galaxy feedback on inter-cluster space remain obscure, and one major impact is the cooling of gas within the region surrounding the galaxy. It has been demonstrated that the inter-cluster space can be cooled by radiation from supernovae and feedback from black holes, but the process is highly dependent on the galaxy's feedback rate. By studying supernova feedback rates greater than $10^{46}$ erg/s, it has been shown that cold gas clouds can form and evolve within this region, influencing their thermodynamic properties. The evolution of these properties is driven by the galaxy's feedback, which causes the cold gas to grow in size, decrease in temperature, increase in density, and increase in pressure. The cold gas can extend up to 10 times the radius of the galaxy, has a mass of millions of solar masses, and has a lifetime of thousands of years. The hot gas is compressed by the cold gas, resulting in a high pressure ratio of hundreds, as well as a high temperature and density ratio of the two gases. The galaxy's feedback, however, causes the cold gas to evaporate, causing the hot gas to decrease in temperature, increase in density, and increase in pressure. The hot gas is compressed by the cold gas, resulting in a high pressure ratio of the two gases. The hot gas, in turn, emits X-rays,

The investigation into the fundamental limits of the P-CP transformation and related concepts is vital in evaluating the P-CP-CP transformation predictions of the Standard Model and exploring phenomena beyond the Standard Model.  In particular, the top qupton, a beyond the standard model particle, influences the CP-violating parameters of the top quark in terms of its interactions and mass.  In this research, the top qupton's impact on the parameters $\phi_{\phi t}^s$, $\phi_{\phi t}^c$, and $\phi_{\phi t}^u$ of the top quark is examined, showing that these parameters can be limited to approximately $0.02$, $0.03$, and $0.02$ respectively, based on the top qupton's mass exceeding $1.15$ TeV.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have a unique twist as they involve the scattering of a particle with high spin, in this case a level-$m$ state with spin $m+2$. The calculated results for levels m=0, m=1 and m=2 have been verified using on-shell recursion techniques. These calculations have also found a surprising connection with the renowned Riemann Zeta function.

The envisioned mobile networks of the future will leverage advanced learning techniques for efficient resource allocation and optimization, coinciding with increasing mobile device and application proliferation. Forecasting and resource planning will become crucial for operators to meet the growing demands of mobile traffic. Deep learning's success in addressing complex, high-dimensional problems has led to its application in diverse real-world scenarios. We outline the potential of applying deep learning to future mobile networks, highlighting specific use cases such as load forecasting and resource optimization. Moreover, we emphasize the importance of addressing challenges within this domain and explore possible solutions to facilitate its adoption in practical settings.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data. To achieve this, we have developed a zero-speech acoustic unit learning method that leverages speaker-dependent emission probabilities for speech encoding. Specifically, we employ a self-organizing neural network to transform speaker-dependent speech into universal acoustic units. The number of these units is predetermined and their emissions are modeled using Gaussian Mixture Models parameters extracted from speaker-independent speech features. The resulting acoustic units are then used as input to a fast speech decoder optimized with a self-organizing neural network. The training data comprises speaker-dependent speech and we evaluate our method using two zero-speech tasks on the DARPA challenges, which involve text-to-speech and speech-to-text operations. The results show that our unit-based approach yields improved signal-to-noise ratio and word error rate compared to speaker-independent speech features, demonstrating its viability for zero-speech synthesis.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle this problem effectively. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are utilized to facilitate optimization across stages. We present a comprehensive framework for multi-limbed robot motion planning that enables the integration of various post-optimization analysis, such as sensitivity examination, to assess the planned motion's feasibility. This framework is demonstrated through simulations of a 7-DoF humanoid robot with flexible joints, including a flexible knee joint, under realistic conditions.

We have developed two comprehensive sets of criteria for achieving a desired quantum state transformation using quantum resource theory principles. The first criterion is a fundamental requirement for all state transformations and is derived from methods previously established for quantum distillation. The second criterion specifically outlines the conditions for achieving a desired state transformation through a straightforward procedure. Together, these criteria serve as necessary and sufficient conditions for the physical transformation between quantum states using an approach known as the one-way distillation protocol. We have applied this approach to the specific case of quantum state purification and determined the precise requirements for achieving this transformation. Furthermore, we have simplified the original condition for purification by representing it as an optimization problem, making the calculation of achievable purifications from a given impure state more efficient.

We investigate the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried in human hands, reduced to a model of a nonlinear pendulum with varying parameters. These parameters are subject to random fluctuations. To analyze this stochastic system, a stochastic averaging method is employed to reduce the order of the equations and express key characteristics of the pendulum's movement as functions of a few variables. The key outcome of this study is a stochastic stability chart that identifies regions of parametric resonance and areas where the random excitations cause the pendulum's movements to amplify significantly.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks. To tackle this problem, we introduce a new method called Distributionally Robust Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DR-DSGD), which accounts for the shift in the joint distribution of local data over time. Regularizing the deviation from the initial joint distribution in terms of entropy ensures the robustness of the distributional model. Analytically, we analyze the convergence of DR-DSGD and provide a theoretical bound on the distributional risk of the minimizer obtained at termination. Comparing with traditional decentralized learning based on Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD), our DR-DSGD offers a trade-off between communication efficiency and robustness. In communication rounds, its requirement is reduced by a factor of O(1/(1 + \lambda T)) of traditional DSGD, where \lambda represents the regularization parameter and T denotes the total number of communication rounds. In addition, we conduct theoretical and simulation-based evaluations of our DR-DSGD, which demonstrates its effectiveness in Drucker-Little traffic prediction and Kernel Mean Embedding based Drucker-Manola distribution classification.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma.

Using the FLASH code, researchers investigated the role of magnetic fields in
magneto-centrifugal jets that form during the collapse of protostars. The study
focused on comparing jets that develop under the influence of weak,
intermediate, and strong magnetic fields. The results showed that a stronger
magnetic field leads to more developed and longer protostellar jets. The
intermediate magnetic field resulted in the most well-defined and collimated jets,
whereas the weak magnetic field produced less defined jets with lower acceleration.
The simulations also indicated that the mass and momentum in these jets are directly
related to the magnetic field strength. Furthermore, the presence of an intermediate
magnetic field resulted in the ejection of more angular momentum, potentially leading
to the formation of longer-disc disks. The comparison with observations revealed that
the FLASH code's predictions for intermediate magnetic fields match the observed
properties of protostellar jets, including their speed, launch angle, and alignment.

This study investigates the optimal balance between performance capabilities and operational limits for a group of nonlinear systems, governed by unknown but model-consistent constraints. To optimize overall team performance, we introduce a performance-safety assessment function that measures the margin of safety for each individual, with its maximum value representing maximum possible performance. We then develop a performance monitoring system that tracks and reports each member's current and desired safety levels to its respective controller, enabling the latter to adjust inputs to maintain safe operations. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that the team's total performance is guaranteed to remain within safe bounds. Furthermore, the proposed evaluation framework can be adaptively adjusted based on the specific constraints of the team's composition, making it applicable to both fixed constraints and dynamic constraints. To illustrate its versatility, we apply our results to the control of a nonlinear team of vehicles under dynamic constraints.

This research focuses on identifying equilibrium points and periodic orbits in a system influenced by the Earth's shape and the solar moon gravitational fields, for objects with a high area-to-mass ratio. The model incorporates the Earth's oblateness effect, represented by the J2 parameter, and its influence on the gravitational anomaly, as well as the solar and lunar gravitational forces, considered proportional to the area-to-mass ratio. The varying oblateness coefficient due to the object's orientation enables exploration of stable equilibrium points and their dependence on the oblateness coefficient parameter in three-dimensional space. The outcomes suggest the existence of additional resonant equilibrium points in certain conditions, in contrast to the traditional Earth-centered system with an expanded gravitational field, which has a maximum of five equilibrium points. The periodic orbits in this system can be analyzed using the continuation method, which involves exploring various area-to-mass and oblateness coefficient parameter combinations. The research findings also highlight an effect of the parameter interaction that causes periodic orbits with unusual behavior, which may have significant implications for future observations and predictions.

We examine the description of periodic tight-binding models under the influence of a time-dependent electromagnetic field, focusing on a two-site unit cell. We derive the Schrieffer-Wolf transformation to transform the Hamiltonian into a moving frame, which serves as a gauge theory formulation. This allows us to compare various descriptions of light-matter interaction in tight-binding models: velocity, dipole, and velocity dipole gauges. We analyze the convergence properties of these descriptions with respect to the Taylor expansion in the field strength and explore their implications for simulating strong-field processes like tunnel ionization and bound-to-free transitions. We find that the velocity dipole gauge has the simplest and most physically intuitive mapping, while the dipole gauge offers a computationally efficient and gauge mapping consistent with the principle of gauge invariance.

In 3D pose and shape estimation, variations within the same class can significantly impact accuracy. Current approaches primarily rely on external cues from specific objects or utilize predefined models to represent objects, but this limits their generalizability to various categories. Our study focuses on in-category 3D pose and shape estimation without a fixed object reference. To address the challenge of intra-class variability, we introduce a new dataset, PASCAL Context, consisting of point clouds with associated poses and shapes from various contexts. Our proposed method employs self-supervised 3D pose and shape estimation by leveraging the contextual points. Based on our novel and diverse dataset, we evaluate the limitations of existing methods and provide a new benchmark.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it in three-dimensional space.

A new approach to accelerating the assessment of innovative therapies in the field of oncology is gaining attention, which involves conducting multi-arm phase II/III basket trials. This method evaluates multiple tumors by sharing treatment assignments based on common molecular characteristics. To address challenges in analyzing such trials with diverse tumor types and uncertain target validation, a simplified statistical model is proposed. This model assumes treatment efficacy is driven by molecular rather than tumor characteristics and allows for the independent selection of control group sample sizes for each arm. This is complemented by the development of an optimal design optimization method. The proposed approach is compared with other methodologies through the use of simulation studies. The results indicate that this method is less efficient when there are a small number of arms. The authors discuss potential implications in the context of a recent basket trial on mRNA vaccines.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, current control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements due to the trade-offs involved. This research introduces an innovative approach to address the issue, focusing on the development of a coupled magnetic-bearing and rotation shaft system. The method leverages a single-channel feedback control to optimize performance and break the limitations of traditional control designs. By utilizing this strategy, precise rotor position can be achieved with minimal distortion, even at high speeds. The effectiveness of the proposed control technique is thoroughly evaluated through comprehensive time- and frequency-domain simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness in meeting the requirements of high-precision motion systems.

We introduce a general approach to aligning large, complex 3D point clouds, often used in robotics and autonomous driving. Our technique innovatively combines keypoint and keyframe detection and aligns them using a hierarchical strategy. This method streamlines the alignment process by breaking it into two manageable stages. To support this approach, we introduce a two-network architecture designed for efficient keypoint and keyframe identification and alignment. Extensive experiments validating our method's effectiveness are presented, including a comparison with existing techniques on standard datasets.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if, for every automorphism $\phi$ of G, the twisted conjugacy classes $Cl_\phi(G)$ contain an infinite number of elements. We identify the group-by-group infinite $R_\infty$ automorphisms for groups within the class of finitely generated nilpotent groups. It's already established that such groups exhibit infinite $R_\infty$ automorphisms when of torsion-free rank at least 2. Here, we demonstrate the existence of these automorphisms even in the case of torsion-free rank one. Additionally, we examine infinite $R_\infty$ automorphisms in the context of finitely generated solvable metabelian groups.

Instead of delving into various assumptions that speculate beyond the Standard Model, we explore how the theory's inherent expectations can clarify the stability of the Higgs potential. One critical factor in this context is the top quark mass, which influences the evolution of the Higgs coupling in high-energy scenarios. We concentrate on how to measure this mass precisely using particle decays within the 8 TeV dataset, specifically through the process $t\bar{t}H$, which involves the Higgs' decay into distinct channels. Our analysis delves into how the signal's shape can provide a more accurate reading of the Higgs mass, underpinning the reliability of our standard model-based predictions.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions and demonstrating that the longitudinal and transverse distribution amplitudes for the kaon are not identical.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within ${S}^{\sigma}_{s}$ and establishes inclusion relationships between different Gelfand-Shilov spaces, as well as their connections to other well-known spaces. It also examines the differentiability properties of functions within ${	ext{Σ}}^{\\sigma}_s$ and proves that this space contains smooth functions for any level of differentiability. The rapid decay of functions within ${S}^{\sigma}_{s}$ leads to the conclusion that any such function can be represented as a convergent power series in any open domain of the complex plane.

Segmentation of new, unlabeled imaging modalities is a significant challenge.
Deep learning-based methods have achieved great success but depend on extensive
manual annotation, which is costly and time-consuming.
Automatic knowledge transfer from pre-trained models to new models offers a
promising solution, yet instance segmentation remains under-explored in this
regard.
We present a novel Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Instance segmentation
(UDAI) framework for cross-modality settings.
Our approach employs Cross-Modality Feature Alignment (CMFA) to optimize the
shared task without access to ground truth, ensuring efficient feature
alignment and reduced information loss.
To recover the instance segmentation generator's weights, we use Kullback-Leibler
divergence and a novel Pseudo Labeling Strategy (PLS) to generate target labels
for the generator.
Our PLS strategy iteratively refines instance segmentation predictions using a
soft-NMS post-processor.
We evaluated UDAI on synthetic and real datasets, including 3D electron
microscopy and MRI and CT images, achieving superior performance over current
methods.
Our UDAI method's code is publicly available at https://github.com/
yechengli/UDAI.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and end-to-end
learning, to achieve future video feature generation and action prediction tasks in a
unified framework through end-to-end end-to-end learning. By utilizing Recurrent
Neural Networks, we can tackle both future action generation and prediction challenges
simultaneously. Our model takes an input video and a time step, transforms the video
using a Convolutional Neural Network, maps the selected features to a radial
basis function space using a novel technique that reduces RNN input dimensions,
and feeds this transformed feature into an RNN with shared weights. During
training, we utilize a novel parameter-sharing method, while making predictions
involves setting the RNN's hidden layer state to the trained feature. Evaluation
results on two action prediction datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our
approach in generating future video actions and predicting actions.

High-energy flares emitted by small stars like M dwarfs and K dwarfs have significant effects on exoplanets through atmospheric changes and surface radiation, and are a key factor in assessing biosignatures. To better understand these stars' flares in various wavelengths, researchers used data from the UVIT instrument on the AstroSat satellite to analyze stellar flares in exoplanet-hosting stars during exoplanet searches. A surprising discovery was made while studying the radiation effects on an exoplanet called ASASINS J1409.33 +6543.0301016113, where the UV flux increase during a flare event exceeded that observed in X-rays. This unique finding suggests potential implications for atmospheric atmospheric chemistry and the presence of life.

A review of G2 and SO(4) cobordism obstacles is provided, with additional examination of nearly parallel G2 structures in relation to real Killing spinors and their connection to the Sobel'ev-Hirzebruch characteristic equation.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies $T\langle x,y\rangle = \langle Tx,y\rangle = \langle x,Ty\rangle = \langle x,T\rangle$. This discussion focuses on C-normal operators on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. We examine the relationship between a given C-normal operator $T$ and its transpose, investigate the spectral properties, determine the Jordan canonical form known as the Chebyshev canonical form, explore matrix representations in an orthonormal basis, and discuss the relationship between finite-dimensional C-normal operators and 2-norms.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions can be modeled by a long walk through a p-vertex graph, with its characteristics dictated by the root at the beginning and the fermion content at the end of the walk. Moreover, the number of such p-core p'-partitions containing a given fixed shape is found using a computationally efficient, recursively determined method.

Neural network-based point cloud models are increasingly being used for various tasks, such as classification and segmentation. These models typically consist of two parts: a network and a module that processes and organizes points in 3D space. The choice of module affects a model's ability to handle points in 3D space, and the lack of standardization can lead to differences in model performance. Through our study, we have developed a standard for evaluating these modules by analyzing their responses to common 3D transformations, and tested the effect of normalization on 12 widely used models. Based on our findings, we have identified the need for a normalization module that enhances the models' robustness, and proposed two general methods for this purpose.

We're investigating the medium access capabilities of Carrier Sense Multiple Access (CSMA) protocols in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks. We're using ALOHA as a reference point and discovering that, due to the nature of radar signals, there's a considerable overlap between signals sent by different radar units, leading to false clear channel assessments. To resolve this challenge, we've developed a measurement report-based protocol, along with we've developed analytical and mathematical methods to evaluate the channel utilization efficiency among radar units, taking into account the effect of signal overlap. We've found through comparison that CSMA protocols generally offer better channel utilization than ALOHA, and our methods provide a straightforward and clear way to measure performance, avoiding the need for difficult numerical integrations.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. A new investigation employs a different approach, examining the interaction of entangled photons from a spectral walk-off type spontaneous parametric down-conversion source with an optical absorption material, illuminated by a continuous-wave laser. The material in question is a malachite-glass plate. Interferometric correlation measurements reveal a significant decrease in spectral correlations in the presence of the material, an effect attributed to entangled two-photon absorption and indicated by an S21 value of 0.00036 plus or minus 0.00009. The statistical significance of the effect is calculated to be 2.2-sigma, considering the added complexity and potential benefits of the proposed detection technique.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre98, given a fixed regularisation in the sense of Rie, is in fact a T-spectral sequence. This finding is achieved through deriving a generalised Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence and precisely defining its E_2-term.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building on the success of neural methods in temporal KC, we conduct a review
of the key technological components in this field, analyzing existing approaches
from both a technical and practical perspective, while highlighting their
respective advantages and limitations. Based on our analysis, we propose
future research directions for the application of neural methods in this field.

The acoustic waves generated when an object strikes the ground can be as disturbing, if not more so, as the sound of the impact itself. In this research, a novel approach is presented to investigate the perceptibility of the sound generated by the interaction between the striking object and the ground surface. The sound produced is analyzed by examining the frequency spectrum resulting from a simulation, and this investigation focuses on the FYE as a key metric. FYE represents the fraction of the total sound energy in a given frequency band that exceeds an audible threshold, and in this research, the threshold is set at 20 micropascals. In this investigation, the ground sound is compared to the sound of the impact itself across a range of impact velocities and projectile masses. Additionally, strategies are proposed to minimize the sound produced by the object's impact on the ground, including using an acoustic damper material.

A class of all-versus-nothing proofs exists that link the behavior of multiple qubits to their joint properties, rendering individual properties meaningless. While previously believed to rely solely on perfect correlations, we've discovered an connection to imperfect correlations, expanding their scope. Notably, this link can be established through a deterministic measurement process on a specific subset of states, known as Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states and related systems, that also yields always-type connections. These findings have been expanded to apply to other comparable systems.

In flat bands, interacting systems lack a definite behavior, leading to a diverse range of possible effects. The lack of research into this area stems from the difficulty in identifying and studying flat bands. Our paper, however, makes a significant contribution by employing machine learning to detect flat bands in varying dimensions. Our approach has been successfully applied to examine the flat band characteristics in the Lieb lattice with modified hopping terms.

A newly discovered two-dimensional material, 2D hydrogen boride monolayer, exhibits potential as a superconductor with potential applications in the development of highly sensitive magnetometers and quantum devices. However, understanding its characteristics in the presence of an external magnetic field is a pressing need. This study explores the influence of magnetic fields on 2D hydrogen boride monolayer's properties, discovering that it can adjust its optical interaction with light and enhance its superconducting capabilities. Additionally, it is found that this material can function as a precise nanoscale sensor of magnetic fields.

Research on the division of numbers into equal parts was conducted, focusing on a specific type of division where the size of each segment is limited to a given value, k. By considering the overall size of each segment as a variable and counting the possible values for the first variable, a new set of values was discovered and linked to a specific number from a mathematical database. To calculate these new values, a mathematical model was developed, and an efficient method for large numbers was also designed. A table of values was created and used to introduce the research, while an interesting property of the numbers was found and an efficient calculation method was designed. Finally, some numbers were calculated and chosen to demonstrate the efficiency of the new method, while an open question for future research was proposed.

We've introduced a novel concept, stiffness, which identifies sets that maintain their characteristics under a system's long-term evolution. This concept's primary purpose is to create an algorithmic method for discovering statistically significant components within systems. Our strategy involves iteratively refining sets with high stiffness until an invariant set with high stiffness is produced. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, we present multiple examples in various systems, including non-computable cases demonstrating the necessity of certain conditions in our theorem.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and complex software systems for redundancy. Driven by cost considerations, the development of these systems has shifted from hardware-based to software-based approaches, which in turn has given rise to numerous software tools for system design and software development. However, these systems' dependability is difficult to guarantee due to the application's high level of sophistication. In this study, we present a comprehensive framework for model-based dependency analysis that enables the formal verification of the dependability of such systems. Our approach incorporates the modeling of functional requirements, software, and hardware, in addition to the evaluation of performance and safety aspects. Using our proposed framework, we can confirm the fail-operability and safety of an automated driving system, specifically an automated emergency braking system, by assessing its dependability.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a'shimmying' threshold. This method's effectiveness is further demonstrated and compared to state-of-the-art methods on numerous real-world systems, with successful application to a previously unresolved problem in the power industry.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different frameworks - whether it be geometric, algebraic or analytical - to represent his thinking. The primary argument in our paper is in support of the viewpoint put forth by Panizzi and Grayson, which is that analytical frameworks are the most accurate means of portraying Leibnizian calculus.

Using the configuration-based emulator called CosmoEmu, an artificial neural network emulator was created to replicate HI intensity mapping simulations. This emulator, trained on full non-biasing physics in the context of Euclid HI tomography, was then used in a likelihood analysis with two- and eight-point power spectrum multipoles at a wavenumber of 0.1 $h$ $\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$. This empirical emulator allows for the efficient constraint of cosmological parameters, enabling the optimal convergence behavior to be leveraged. With two- and eight-point power spectrum multipoles, six cosmological parameters can be accurately constrained: the present matter density, sound horizon, primordial spectral index, non-Gaussianity, a dynamical dark energy model parameter, and a evolution parameter. This results in the68\% confidence intervals, respectively, of (-0.022, 0.022), (0.97, 1.03), (0.02, 0.2), and (0.03, 0.08).

Given a power-bounded operator $T$ on a Banach space $X$, and a sequence of vectors $x_0, x_1, \ldots$ that arises from iterating $T$ applied to a single vector $z$, where $x_n = T^nz$, the article proves that if this sequence is linearly independent, the resulting Banach space is never flat. In other words, if the sequence isn't uniformly bounded below or above in a certain sense, applying $T$ to a particular vector will cause both the lower and middle mean values to diverge to 0 and infinity, respectively.

Learning recommenders in dynamic environments where the distribution of data shifts over time is particularly challenging. Over time, the accumulating preference data can lead to the shift in the overall distribution and the decline in the recommender system's performance. In this study, we introduce an online learning framework for collaborative filtering that addresses the issue of non-stationarity in the data. Using an adaptive weighting approach, our method assigns a dynamic weight to the loss calculated on the aggregated historical preference data, based on the current user's interaction. This weight update allows our algorithm to effectively learn from incoming data and maintain its performance in changing environments. Theoretical evaluation shows that the proposed algorithm has a bound on regret and mean deviation that scales linearly with the time step and also considers the complexity of the loss function. In addition, our evaluation demonstrates that the proposed algorithm outperforms the baseline algorithms and achieves better accuracy and serendipity compared to the offline counterpart.

From the perspective of random matrix theory, asymptotic freeness explains why
certain products of matrices exhibiting specific statistical characteristics result
in matrices with predictable statistical properties. Additionally, asymptotic
freeness clarifies why, for instance, the sum of two symmetric matrices also
maintains symmetry. This paper investigates the asymptotic freeness of certain
transformed quadratic forms of random diagonal matrices and a common stochastic
vector. By applying a new variant of the semi-circular distribution and an
infinite divisutable distribution related to the Poisson-Lukacs distribution, we
derive limiting distributions for specific statistical properties. We verify these
findings by conducting numerical simulations.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods that produce concise summaries of execution relevance within timed universes. These universes are modeled as products of the clock behavior and an underlying temporal sequence. By breaking the problem into two components - determining if sequence descriptions match a specified priority automaton and extracting significant sequence sections - we develop two corresponding solution approaches. The former utilizes a previously established algorithm for prioritized regular expression evaluation, whereas the latter employs a technique for prioritized summarization of sequence sections in relation to a given priority automaton.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined through the lens of isospin breaking, with emphasis on
the conversion of the $f_0(980)$ into $a_0(980)$. This conversion is driven
by isospin violation stemming from both charged-current interactions and
flavor-singlet octet mixing. An investigation of the impact of isospin breaking
on the difference in branching ratios of $\bar B_s^0 \to \psi J/f$ and $\bar B_s^0
\to \psi, a_0(980)$ reveals that it could be observable experimentally.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to enhance the performance of the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI). Its guide mode tracks the telescope, the low-order wavefront sensing mode measures wavefront distortions, the nulling mode suppresses strong starlight, and the imaging mode captures scientific images. A novel calibration technique for the nulling mode was developed to compensate for system imperfections. A major challenge in this area is the lack of a dark reference, as blocking the starlight results in minimal signal due to the system's low efficiency. A more effective solution involves using a low-cost, in-orbit satellite as an isotropic dark source. A successful experiment using the GSAT-1 satellite to measure wavefront distortions and a fringe pattern demonstrates the feasibility of this technique despite the satellite's low signal strength.

We examine the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem in the context of a graph, where n vertices and e edges are defined by associated costs and vertex demands. Given k supplier vertices and an outlier parameter k, the objective is to minimize either non-supplier vertex removal costs or inaccessible cost by connecting some supplier vertices to all other vertices.
