In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude. To understand this phenomenon, we have developed a delayed time-fractional Fisher-KPP equation, a model whose base, introducing delay into a system, exhibits typical features of non-analytical, non-local, and fractional characteristics. By analyzing the system's travel waves, we find that this time-fractional wavefront becomes local when the delay is periodically modulated, a phenomenon we attribute to the system's self组织 property. What is more, the time-fractional system allows for an explanation of the hole burning effect, a process where a system's diffusion is restricted to specific points in time, effectively creating a time-crystal where the system's delay is crystalized.

We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018).

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. A potential solution involves applying "design mining" to annotate developer discussions automatically. This process could be facilitated by a potential technique that uses contextual metadata to categorize these interactions as related to software design. Research in this area has demonstrated the effectiveness of metadata-based profiling for context-aware filtering and recommendation systems; similar approaches have been shown to be valuable in the field of design mining as well.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.
Dark energy and dark matter result from a separation of virtual particles at a boundary created by a large-scale structure in the universe. The pressure exerted by the virtual particles inside the boundary contributes to dark energy, while the pressure of the particles outside the boundary contributes to a form of dark matter. As this boundary expands, the density of dark energy remains constant, resulting in the Davis-Martynov equation. The model also suggests that the density of dark matter will eventually reach a final value, causing the density ratio to remain finite in a future "Big Freeze" scenario.

Proximal methods are a popular approach for optimizing nonsmooth functions due to its versatility in handling different norms, but it often suffers from slow convergence, 
a key area that needs improvement. A new framework is proposed to enhance the proximal method by integrating it with the Frank-Wolter technique, 
allowing the proposal to utilize the best bound for nonsmooth optimization problems and achieve faster convergence. The feasibility of this new framework 
is demonstrated through applications to various norms-based optimization problems, and its performance is confirmed through experiments.

We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. This generalized idea then leads to the definition of weakly special $1$-absorbing prime ideals. Characterizations of strong and weakly special $1$-absorbing prime ideals are provided, along with an examination of their applicability to Noetherian rings. Specifically, we are looking at the relationship between strong weakly special $1$-absorbing prime ideals and the associated prime ideals of the ideal generated by the product of three elements in a ring with identity.

We present new measurements of the total decay probabilities of B+ to rho+(nu) and B0 to rho-(nu) as well as the decay of B+ to rho0(nu), combining results from two different methods to achieve the most precise estimates available. Analysis of data collected by LHCb from runs 1 and 2 of the LHC, totaling 189 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity, was utilized to obtain these estimates. The calculated decay probabilities are (2.43 0.64 0.36) x 10^-5, 1.50 (+0.41 (-0.37)) x 10^-5, and (+-0.74 (-0.46)) x 10^-5 respectively, with separate calculations considering only signal and also accounting for background.

Our approach utilizes photonic devices in spectroscopy to efficiently screen medications and support clinical diagnosis by detecting the presence of multiple substances in quick succession. By matching these photonic devices with machine learning algorithms, we can enhance clinical diagnostic capabilities. We've successfully utilized this approach to screen for multiple sugar present, identifying their types and quantities with exceptional accuracy and speed. Our method's scalability allows for the rapid evaluation of spectroscopy with hundreds of photonic devices, ensuring cost-effective and timely medication screening. Our study successfully demonstrates this approach in identifying seven types of sugars with high accuracy and speed. Our study further highlights the potential for scaling this approach in screening hundreds of substances simultaneously. Our study clearly shows that these photonic devices in spectroscopy offer a faster and more efficient alternative to traditional methods. Our study clearly indicates the potential for scaling this approach in identifying hundreds of substances at once. Our study clearly demonstrates the potential for these photonic devices in spectroscopy to support medical diagnosis. Our study clearly indicates the potential for these photonic devices in supporting medical diagnosis.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

Several local authorities face challenges in efficiently and effectively managing automated road damage assessment. While several software solutions exist, they often lack essential features or require substantial modification to meet specific requirements, which can be costly. Our research presents a free, open-source solution tailored to the needs of municipalities for classifying road damage and collecting additional metadata. We also discuss the essential elements for customizing road classification systems to meet the specific needs of different users.

Imitation learning is a highly efficient training method in reinforcement learning (RL) that bypasses the need to assign an accurate reward function. Instead, it can directly learn optimal policies from expert demonstrations. In contrast, traditional reward-augmented Multi-agent RL is plagued by several key issues, such as the difficulty of defining precise reward functions, its sensitivity to changes, and the problem of reward sparsity. To address these limitations, researchers are exploring multi-agent imitation learning. This approach is, however, hindered by the scarcity of full-state observations in demonstrated trajectories, as obtaining such detailed information is often impractical. To overcome this scarcity, defining state in terms of what an agent perceives, rather than its world state, is a more natural and accurate description. Consequently, imitation learning based on agent perceptions is both essential and natural. Nevertheless, it is an open question how to effectively learn from agent-perception-based demonstrations in the context of multi-agent RL. To answer this question, a novel multi-agent imitation learning framework called State-From-Action (SFA) is proposed. The SFA framework overcomes the high dimensionality and complexity of world states by representing them as sequences of action permutations. By representing world states through action sequences, the SFA framework enables agents to learn a comprehensive understanding of the world's state from just these sequences in their demonstrated trajectories. By relying solely on agent-perceived states, the SFA framework eliminates the need for full-world-state observations, rendering it practical for a

A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first stars lies in the scope of their radiative feedback capabilities during the early universe. One promising area of research is the role of magnetic fields in star formation, particularly in the primordial context, which remains largely unexplored. To address this research gap, we conducted magnetohydrodynamic simulations of star formation in metal-poor, dense clouds under M cosmic microwave background radiation. The simulations were conducted under an expanding universe model with the M cosmic microwave background radiation in equilibrium. The magnetized clouds were initially in hydrostatic equilibrium before the M cosmic microwave background radiation was expanded, triggering their gravitational collapse. The simulations revealed that the collapse triggered by magnetism is significantly more efficient and results in more powerful radiative feedback compared to nonmagnetic cases. The amplification of the magnetic field strength is also found to be greater and the magnetic field aligns along the collapse direction. It is observed that this leads to the formation of mass gaps, a mass-dependent mass loss, and the disruption of the mass spectrum as a result of feedback. The collapse in the magnetic context is found to be more rapid, and the mass of the protostar is significantly lower and the mass dependence of the luminosity is shallower. The accretion of gas onto the protostar is significantly hindered by magnetic fields, and a more massive seed protostar is required to restore the mass dependence of the luminosity through accretion, thereby potentially reducing the impact of feedback in

Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves comparing two properties of an object, identified through Attribute Values, to establish relationships. The strength and relevance of these relationships are assessed through confidence and support, respectively. We explore the process of deriving association rules using Python's Apriori algorithm and demonstrate that increasing the minimum confidence threshold results in associations with higher confidence, but may reduce the number of valid associations due to decreased support. Conversely, lowering the threshold yields associations with smaller confidence and often insignificant support, such as those with a count of one. Increasing the minimum support also produces associations with higher confidence, as more data points contribute to the calculation. However, many associations may still be considered noise due to low confidence and small support counts. Selecting an optimal association therefore requires carefully choosing appropriate minimum confidence and support thresholds, as well as the number of items to compare. Higher confidence and support levels lead to fewer but more significant associations, while lower levels produce associations with smaller confidence and support, some of which may be noise.

Individuals within the criminal justice system who have mental health issues often need to be treated to reduce the long-term harm they experience.  However, it is often unclear how such treatments impact the likelihood of offenders returning to the criminal justice system following their release from a custodial institution.  To address this ambiguity, researchers examined whether mental health treatment during the probation period affects the secondary reoffending rate.  Using data from the Health Improvement Network in the UK, the researchers analyzed secondary reoffending patterns in the census cohort of 1,151,758 offenders who were on probation between 2008 and 2017.  The researchers used a difference-in-difference approach to compare mental health treatment and control groups, while controlling for various confounding variables such as age, sex, prior offending history, and the type of primary offense.  The researchers found that mental health treatment during the probation period reduced the secondary reoffending rate among all offenders by 10% and had an even larger impact on offenders at high risk of secondary reoffending, reducing their risk by 21%.  The researchers concluded that providing mental health treatment to offenders at high risk of secondary reoffending during their probation period could significantly decrease the burden on the criminal justice system and healthcare services in the long-term.  The researchers suggest incorporating the impact of mental health treatment into a cost-benefit analysis of secondary prevention programs, such as the census.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to enhance the current systems' ability to currently as aware of their surroundings. They will be crucial for various applications, including millimeter-wave and future communication technologies, though they also present challenges in acquisition and maintenance. This work leverages metaverse-based data to simplify creating and obtaining accurate radio maps. It utilizes commercial UAVs to collect data while navigating the metaverse for virtual training, after which human users collect a user-specific dataset via a commercial drone during their flight. This enables accurate estimation of their current location within the metaverse and precise signal strength prediction without needing to actually transmit. We further utilize this approach to predict and determine the location within the metaverse without knowing the user's current location, after which they are directly localized via RANSAC. The proposed method was evaluated using a realistic dataset, achieving excellent results in both location estimation and metaverse-based data analysis with low error margins of less than 5 meters RMS.

This paper outlines a novel approach called ATSA4HMM4W, designed to detect and
characterize unusual patterns in time-series data using Hidden Markov Models (HMMs).
It adapts a previously proposed framework for dynamic time-warped clustering and
extends it to accommodate multiple completely observed state transition models.
Two methods for inferring the warping paths of hidden and visible states are provided.
Additionally, ATSA4HMM4W employs a sliding window technique to create sub-sequence
models from normal data, enabling the identification of mismatches between new
sub-sequence observations and these pre-established models to flag potential
anomalies. The paper also discusses how varying the size of the sliding window
can impact the system's sensitivity and mentions the possibility of automating this
parameter selection process. The paper concludes with experimental results using real-life
electroencephalogram data to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

This research introduces and investigates advanced verification systems that utilize three distinct modalities to confirm a person's identity. Building upon this concept, we developed and implemented a robust platform to efficiently compare the performance of unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal systems in end-to-end neural networks. The chosen modalities are audio, visual, and textual features extracted from social media posts and online profiles. All modalities are incorporated into a single neural network that is trained in a end-to-end manner, and the dataset, termed MVBench, is introduced, consisting of approximately 10000 profiles from multiple platforms. Our experiments demonstrate a notable increase in accuracy with the integration of additional modalities, with the most effective configuration being a system incorporating all three, that outperforms even human verification in accuracy and is fully automated and digital-based in nature.

The primary goal of this research is to investigate the most effective methods for enhancing Transformer and Conformer models via additional training. We focus on data augmentation in the context of automatic speech recognition and propose using Large-Batch Training with Augmented Data (LBA), which involves mixed random augmentation techniques such as time-mirror, time-squeeze, spectral, noise, and warping. We find that LBA Lora and continued training with augmented data yield the best results, surpassing the performance of our baseline model by a significant margin of 2.1 WER in the semi-supervised scenario on the LibriSpeech test-clean corpus.

The maximum likelihood approach can yield multiple solutions, and a generalized maximum likelihood estimator is developed to resolve the ambiguity of mixing distributions and their related random measures based on observable data. Under specific conditions, it has been proven that the generalized maximum likelihood estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal.

From a specific approach to protecting privacy, known as differential privacy, researchers have introduced various modifications, such as One-Sided Differential Privacy and Controlling Characteristic Differential Privacy. However, implementing one-sided approaches to protect privacy is complicated due to the difficulty in quantifying noise for an asymmetrical purpose. To simplify this process, we introduce an adaptation of the controlling characteristic approach tailored for one-sided data protection, termed COCDP. By leveraging this framework, we can count the number of possible concepts consistent with an dataset, thereby enabling the calculation of appropriate noise. To demonstrate the feasibility of this new approach, we apply COCDP to count discrete values, estimate means and calculate tail counts.

In protoplanetary disks, it is essential to understand the behavior of gas substructures, especially in systems with developing planets. Researchers employed the FORS2 telescope on the VLTI to examine the protoplanetary disk of HR 87AL for gas substructures. They found an unexpected bright spot near 3 AU from the star, and also detected outer ring bright spots at 29 and 42 AU. By analyzing thermal emission patterns, researchers estimated that the inner bright spot contains particles approximately 2-3 AU in size, and that the outer ring has similar particle sizes of 2.5-4 AU. It's hypothesized that these features result from a developing planet at the 12 AU orbit triggering a gravitational instability. Additionally, particles in HR 87AL appear to migrate outward over time, and their colors indicate metal-rich material. This discovered planet-triggered gravitational instability provides further evidence supporting the MHD disk wind model.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis. Leveraging an integrated development environment-based framework, our software enables the development of high-performance analysis tools and allows for seamless extension with custom functions and parameters. The open-source nature of ETA facilitates collaboration and continuous improvement from the user community.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with first-order constraints.

Recent analyses of Gaia data have identified numerous stellar "strings" and "superstructures" in our galaxy. Researchers have proposed the existence of these structures as a result of the merging of dwarf galaxies with the Sun's neighborhood a few billion years ago, allowing the gravitational disruption of these bodies to shape the stellar distribution in the galaxy. 

A novel and straightforward statistical approach is used to measure the significance of these stellar "strings." When applied to the data, this method indicates that certain widely known structures, such as the Helmi "strings," hold a statistically strong link to the Helmi dwarf galaxy. In contrast, it suggests that the majority of other stellar "strings" do not originate from Helmi. 

It has been discovered that the characteristics of these stellar "strings" change significantly depending on the underlying model and dataset used, indicating they are more likely to be random, spreading structures within the galaxy rather than distinct physical formations. 

Furthermore, this analysis fails to detect a substantial connection between these stellar "strings" and the recently discovered GD-1 galaxy, contradicting previous claims that these structures are Helmi in origin. 

Finally, this research does not entirely dismiss the possibility that these stellar "strings" are related to the Galarus galaxy discovered a few years ago, although it does suggest a weak connection.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmonize with one another based on factors like style, type, and color. Recent advancements in fashion recommendation have primarily focused on color coordination, disregarding crucial aspects of visual compatibility.色值匹配. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a technique called Style-T-C-O-Match, which incorporates type, color, and various visual characteristics of an item to calculate a comprehensive similarity score between garments. Sty-T-C-O-Match is an extension of the successful HMLB color matching approach, incorporating type, pattern, and texture comparisons. Color features include saturation, lightness, and the primary color pair, in addition to hue. Pattern and texture analysis employs Gabor filter bank feature extraction and a deep convolutional network, Inception-v2, respectively. Experiments on the IN-Street Fashion dataset reveal that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art multimodal matching methods, yielding a significant 14.6% improvement in Inception-v2 visual features and a substantial 10.4% advantage over style-transfer baselines.

In the framework of quantum resource theory, the evaluation of the optimal resource value of a state is hindered by the lack of clear numerical indicators to categorize non-resource states from resource-rich ones. To overcome this challenge, a novel approach is proposed that assigns a distinct resource type to states exhibiting resource-like properties, facilitating precise differentiation between these two state categories. This method is then exemplified through the analysis of asymptotic conversion in a specific quantum resource theory context.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, the problem of coordinating updates via the central server becomes a considerable challenge. The fully decentralized approach, although eliminating the need for a central server, significantly reduces sample diversity due to a limited number of devices providing updates per iteration. An iterative voting protocol is proposed in this work, aiming to balance these trade-offs. The authors analyze the behavior and performance of the voting protocol in the context of stochastic gradient descent and show that the influence of outdated updates diminishes as the number of active devices increases, thereby reducing the communication overhead between devices and server. Moreover, the authors conduct a large-scale evaluation of the voting protocol across nearly 10K Amazon Kindles, 100 Android phones, and 130 Macbooks, revealing that it can achieve a 30X improvement in throughput over the federated averaging approach, and a 5X improvement in comparison to the fully decentralized approach, while maintaining similar model accuracy.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators.

Recent research has highlighted the connection between the hierarchy of scales and the behavior of black holes across different dimensions. We've explored the hierarchy of dimensions model in the context of a five-dimensional space with one extra dimension of varying characteristics. To represent this complexity, we employed the transverse noncommutative geometry approach. The hierarchy of a particular dimension is determined by a conformal factor, which also influences the rate of Hawking radiation. We've calculated the corrections to the standard four-dimensional radiation rate and analyzed the influence of the hidden dimension on the radiation process. We've discovered that the hierarchy of the dark dimension has a significant impact on the rate of Hawking radiation and the phase transition of supersymmetric black holes. Furthermore, the flat character of the hidden dimension leads to an enhancement of the rate of Hawking radiation.

A experimental investigation into the failure of a particle raft floating on an expanding liquid substrate is conducted. By gradually increasing the liquid's surface area, the changes in raft shape before failure are systematically examined. It is found that the initial deflation of an expanded raft creates a circular sink hole at its center, which eventually leads to a transition of the raft's edge from a flat to a curved morphology. In regions away from the center, the raft's edge forms a series of increasingly large concave features. Failure occurs when the raft's edge fragments into a patterned structure, with the spacing of these fragments increasing towards the raft's edge. The fragmentation pattern is also present in empty raft sections surrounding the central sink hole. The central feature of our discovery is that the spacing between adjacent raft fragments at the time of breaking corresponds to the size of the curved undulations on the flat raft regions. This suggests that raft failure involves local, rather than a wave-like propagation, of a transition from a curved to negative curvature. The existing theory of dislocation pinning is modified to account for the pinning of multiple topological defects, which is consistent with our findings.

The group III nitride class exhibits considerable diversity in its bandgap, making it suitable for various applications from UV to IR wavelengths. However, the material's limited compatibility with gallium arsenide and silicon substrates restricts the development of high-quality gallium nitride layers. In particular, the extremely heavy hole bands of gallium nitride at room temperature resemble those of p-type silicon, which has a nearly identical crystal structure. To overcome these limitations, silicon substrates can be strained when applying a film of gallium nitride, resulting in increased hole band energies. This gain in energy surpasses the effects of strain induced by epitaxial growth of silicon carbide, which has been applied in the development of group III-V silicon optoelectronics, thus making it an ideal platform for further integration of these materials.

Our novel TD learning approach incorporates model-based regression using Gaussian Process (GP) to manage uncertainty in perception, allowing a robot to learn an optimal navigation path within familiar areas despite uncertain marine environments. By using a simple policy, our method avoids complex value function updates and can be implemented in real-time on robotic platforms. In marine navigation tasks, we employ GP regression to model the relationship between the robot's location and its corresponding measurements. This enables us to manage the uncertainty in the robot's perception, and thus, to determine whether the policy is actionable. Through our approach, we enable a robot to learn in familiar areas where the GP model is reliable, and learn to navigate within marine environments.

We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential does not meet the conditions to be considered holomorphic. Consequently, the Hopf differential is zero at certain points, causing the surface's curvature to vanish in those areas. Building on previous work by Cazabat and Pedit on isothermic surfaces, we focus here on describing all isothermic surfaces under these conditions, translating their geometry into the language of soliton surfaces and applying it to describe these surfaces through a Weingarten frame and a loop group method.

We analyze the conditional expectation operator or $L^2$-operator within the framework of Hilbert-Schmidt operators. It is demonstrated that the conditional expectation operator approximates an finite-rank Hilbert-Schmidt operator, which can be computed through an elementary numerical method involving Karhunen-Loève decomposition. Furthermore, we establish mathematical relationships between approximation errors and the behavior of the corresponding conditional variance operator. This relationship is employed to develop numerical methods for estimating the conditional variance operator and its Hilbert-Schmidt norm. These methods are implemented using an open-source Python implementation.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind. We explore and define the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and establish their key properties, including recurrence relations, identities, inequalities and computational methods. We also introduce a specific property related to monotonicity in these analogues and provide their lambda generating functions. Furthermore, we investigate the properties and present recurrence relations for the $\lambda$-weighted sums of the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind.

The development of large-scale knowledge graph embeddings has led to various promising applications. Nevertheless, existing approaches often overlook the temporal scope of entities and relations, resulting in a generalization of facts that may not be suitable for temporal datasets. In this study, we introduce a novel method called Temporal Knowledge Graph Embedding with Scope Awareness (TKE4S), which incorporates the temporal context of entities and relations to improve knowledge graph embeddings. Our approach enables more accurate representations and mitigates over-smoothness in embeddings by leveraging the temporal scope. Moreover, our framework allows for the creation of personalized entity embeddings by incorporating time-varying features. The effectiveness of TKE4S is demonstrated in various benchmark datasets, including Mobius, Knowlectrage, and MedTime.

Cuntz-Krocker-Effros' theorem establishes a direct correlation between strong shift equivalence of row-finite graphs and the isomorphism of their associated C*-algebras. This relationship is further explored and extended through an investigation into a specific type of graph called an extended graph. Specifically, we define the concept of partial shift equivalence, demonstrating its implications on C*-algebras for a particular subset of graph classes, including Leavitt path algebras. Additionally, we introduce the notion of crossed products involving group actions on finite graph C*-algebras, revealing a connection between strong shift equivalence and crossed product C*-algebra isomorphism. A concrete example serves to disprove a previously proposed conjecture regarding this relationship.

In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions.

This study develops a comprehensive framework for assessing the capabilities of Language Models in the task of answering questions over open domains. The evaluation involves both evaluating and fine-tuning these models, with a specific focus on how Language Models can be enhanced through external knowledge sources. To understand the limits of Language Models in this context, we have created a large-scale dataset consisting of 20,000 instances. Additionally, we have designed and implemented a simple yet effective knowledge-aware question answering method based on the T5 model. Experimental results show that our method successfully retrieves accurate answers from pre-trained models by incorporating external knowledge from a knowledge graph. Finally, a thorough analysis of the proposed framework and method is provided, including multiple ablation studies.

We develop a comprehensive understanding of high dimensional expanders by introducing an efficient link between local and global expander properties. As extensions of one-dimensional expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a crucial role in various technological applications and theoretical concepts. Our research utilizes a common framework to describe both local and global expander properties, enabling us to establish a novel relationship between them. This approach is based on a unified system of covering terms and operators that characterize a specific connection coefficient, thereby providing an alternative way to define expander graphs in higher dimensions. Consequently, the bound on this connection coefficient determines their respective quantities, and under specific conditions, we derive precise inequalities that relate the two properties.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing answer options and those not utilized during pre-training exhibit notable performance enhancements.

We have computed the Benois $\mathcal{L}$-invariants for weight one cuspforms and their corresponding representations, and extended this to certain weight zero cuspforms using a connection to the one-forms appearing in Benois's definition of the $\mathcal{E}$-invariant for motivic $L$-functions. Additionally, our work involves explicitly solving the first cohomology group of applicable cuspmodules.

We suggest an innovative method for detecting complex microwave signals using Rydberg atoms, which can accurately identify multiple frequencies simultaneously while maintaining robustness against various electric field influences. Rydberg atoms' heightened sensitivity to electromagnetic fields makes them ideal for precise measurements. In our proposed setup, we utilize two distinct transitions to detect a multitone signal, thereby bypassing the need to know the relative electric field strengths, thereby reducing susceptibility to disturbances. Furthermore, we develop an advanced detection algorithm based on machine learning that substantially improves the determination of frequency components.

UGC 8839, a low surface brightness spiral galaxy, is characterized by extensive star formation occurring far from its central region. The motion of its interstellar gas has been extensively studied, but its origin and the influence of star formation on the galaxy's dynamics remain poorly understood. By utilizing CO emission data, we have created a kinetic distance map, which indicates that CO intensity is closely linked to the distribution of massive star-forming regions rather than the galaxy's global gas motion. Furthermore, we have observed that this effect is most pronounced in regions where local star formation is particularly intense. CO velocity dispersion is also localized in these areas and significantly impacts the galaxy's kinematic distance, making these regions appear more extremely off-axis than they truly are. Our findings imply that the extreme star formation in UGC 8839, whether driven by gravity or turbulence, has an even greater effect on the galaxy's global dynamics.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range of 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under a specific growth constraint.

Using the Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer on the Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution mission, we've observed gravity waves between 2020 and 270 km in altitude and between 2020 and 2022 Pa of pressure. We focused on the horizontal wind component's gravitational wave component, averaging data over 12-hour and 24-hour periods based on local time. We used an auto-spectral method to calculate wave amplitudes, taking into account varying frequencies. Our analysis revealed that wave intensity in the horizontal wind component is significantly influenced by wind speed, albedo, solar flux, and atmospheric turbulence in the mesosphere. We observed that wave intensity in the vertical wind component is influenced by the depth of the well mixed cloud and is in line with what was found for Cassini in the moon's equator. We've found that wave intensity in the horizontal wind component is about an order of magnitude stronger than in the vertical wind component, peaking in the mesosphere at around 80 km. We've detected seasonal variations in the wave intensity in the horizontal wind component, with a clear pattern of higher intensity in the summer months. This is likely due to the role of the general circulation in the planet's atmosphere. We've detected a clear pattern of the zonal mean wind influencing the propagation of the gravitational waves in the atmosphere.

The LHC has undergone over ten years of varied experiments involving photon-photon and photon-nucleus collisions. In particular, ultra-peripheral collisions, where impact parameters exceed the nuclear radius, provide a unique environment for studying these interactions. When the nucleus moves rapidly transversely, it generates a stream of virtual photons, enabling the study of photon-nucleon interactions without hadronic activity in the central region. As of now, the LHC has collected data with four distinct detectors, allowing us to present updated limits on new physics involving the production of light Higgs-like scalars via the decay of heavier scalars, coupled with photons, under considerations of photon-photon fusion and photon-photon initial states.

Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through deep learning have made significant advancements. A significant challenge with current methods is their inability to indicate the class of sound being created. This issue is particularly pertinent in the case of the new model we propose. Our model excels at generating a diverse range of sound effects, extending beyond the typical capabilities of neural audio models. It exhibits distinct audio characteristics, including rooster crows, glass breaking, gunshots, rainfall, gunner laughter, and animal sounds. The model's capacity to generate a vast library of distinct sound effects positions it as a valuable tool for audio data augmentation. It also reveals that a single third-order differential network can effectively produce a multitude of sound effects.

Recurrent networks have gained significant popularity in handling sequential data such as time series and natural language due to their ability to retain memory and apply it to subsequent inputs. They have proven effective in a wide range of applications including speech recognition, translation, and more. However, the performance of these networks is often hindered by the difficulty in leveraging past information due to the instability of training recurrent equations. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed several techniques including orthogonalization and layer-by-layer training. Another method involves parametrisation of recurrent matrices using structured matrices with limited degrees of freedom. This study explores the potential of quasi-triangular matrices as a way to stabilize recurrent networks without incurring excessive parameter overhead. We evaluate the effectiveness of this method on a set of benchmarks and find it to be comparable with other stability techniques. Furthermore, the results indicate that quasi-triangular matrices may even outperform standard recurrent units in some cases.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under economic irreversibility results in an overly aggressive health policy that neglects economic consequences. We develop a model that incorporates two key elements: a more nuanced understanding of how behavior changes in response to economic costs, and a regulatory framework that takes economic trade-offs into account when designing a optimal balancing act between health and economic goals.

The development of modern machine learning techniques has enabled the creation of high-quality models; however, the transparency of their decision-making processes often remains unclear. In many cases, understanding the reasons behind a model's training outcome is as important as the outcome itself. A potential solution to this issue is the computation of Shapley values, which can be used to break down the complexities of model training into more understandable components. Although Monte Carlo-based approaches exist, they are generally impractical due to their reliance on extensive computational resources and insufficient explanation of the underlying complexity of the problem. To address these issues, we propose a method that utilizes learned neural networks to efficiently compute Shapley values, along with a framework for modeling the complexity of the problem, thereby enabling more accurate and reliable estimations. Our proposed framework is flexible and can be adapted to a variety of scenarios, allowing for the estimation of Shapley values even in the absence of a model's parameters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on two real-world image classification datasets, thereby showcasing its potential for promoting transparency in machine learning.

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices.

In an experiment on Mn$_3$Ge, researchers found that pressure significantly influenced the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) due to a rapid decrease in carrier mobility, despite AHE initially increasing at low pressures. The study revealed a direct linear relationship between pressure and both magnetic order and interband gap energy, explaining the initial rise in AHE. A high pressure of 11.5 GPa suppressed the AHE at the Curie temperature by 4 orders of magnitude, explaining earlier findings of the AHE's pressure-dependent sign change. Additionally, a theoretical explanation has been proposed for AHE's initial increase with pressure.

Natural Language Processing's key task, Relation Extraction, identifies pairs of related concepts within a text body. The challenge lies in the vast number of potential concept combinations, which increases quadratically. Current methods struggle to scale for large-scale datasets, but an emerging approach utilizing pre-trained models has improved performance, still falling short of optimal results. Although pre-trained language models capture semantic representations effectively, they fail to consider the specific relationship between concepts. To address this limitation, we propose a two-stage method that first pinpoints relevant concepts and then refines the relationship using pre-trained models. Our approach successfully demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on three datasets, showcasing its potential and demonstrating robustness in handling negative relationships.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary.

We investigate the applications of hypergraphs, an advanced modeling approach, to represent complex systems, an approach that has garnered interest among physicists, in contrast to those who typically use standard graph representations. We develop a general method for translating standard graph properties into hypergraphs, enabling the analysis of hypergraphs, an approach that has yet to be explored, and apply it to the small-world and free percolation models. Our findings reveal that hypergraphs exhibit distinct characteristics, potentially offering new insights into the study of complex systems.

In medical radiology, precise identification and localisation of anatomical structures are vital for diagnosing and treating patients. However, scanning patients takes time and resources, resulting in medical images being filled with unnecessary empty space, which also includes sensitive anatomical information for privacy reasons. Prior research has explored the benefits of incorporating anatomical information for analysis, but for many conditions, these structures are irrelevant. Our work presents a comprehensive study on pre- and post-annotated medical images, investigating the impact of removing empty space and irrelevant anatomy on the performance of deep learning models across various medical tasks.

Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds could reach any positive multiple of the manifold's Euler class. Subsequent studies have shown that this finding can be adapted to tight contact structures in certain manifolds. Our investigation expands upon this line of research by demonstrating that, given a hyperbolic 3-manifold, any tight contact structure on its mapping torus can be deformed into a taut foliation with a specific Euler class, effectively filling the gap between what was known for taut foliations and contact structures.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures.

This paper investigates the suitability of cryptocurrencies for storing value by examining their ability to maintain a stable price. A comprehensive analysis of over 3 million cryptocurrency transactions involving 19 leading digital currencies and their counterparts in nine different countries is conducted using a robust measure of price stability. The study employs a cutting-edge blockchain data analysis technique and covers various cryptocurrency transactions across diverse geographic regions. The results indicate that cryptocurrencies generally do not provide significant protection against inflation when compared to major financial assets, although their price stability relative to the US dollar is comparable to that of foreign currencies in times of high inflation. Notably, the analysis highlights the exceptional stability of Decentralized Finance (DeFi) tokens initially denominated in US dollars. The study's findings are further enriched by an in-depth review of related literature, consideration of potential biases and limitations, and exploration of the economic implications of using cryptocurrencies as a store of value, particularly in reference to the digital dollar.

By integrating analytical methods with numerical techniques, we resolve the KPZ equation's equation of motion in a network of clocks, revealing the large deviation paths and an exact solution for its rate function. Techniques from Hamilton-Jacobi dynamics and Hamiltonian analysis are applied to understand the equation's behavior, resulting in the derivation of a second-order Hamiltonian that yields a exact solution for large deviations. These methods are also used to investigate the rate function in detail. Additionally, we analyze the rate function as the clock factor approaches zero, demonstrating its asymptotic behavior. Our approach is validated by a comparison of the exact solution for large deviations with the KPZ universality class's second-class particle solution.

The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed with data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. Utilizing both in-situ measurements and kinetic simulations, researchers investigate the dynamics and structures of this phenomenon. By applying advanced multivariate methods to in-situ data, where necessary multivariate coherence and multivariate phase spectra are calculated. The results are compared to fully periodic, realistically composed, and slab turbulence simulations. In the observed and simulated spectra, distinct behaviors are evident at both perpendicular and parallel wave numbers. The phase spectra reveal correlated variations between observed plasma components, consistent with turbulent structures seen in simulations at certain wave-number thresholds. The correlation patterns are also consistent with those seen in simulations at certain wave-number thresholds. The observed and simulated phase-coherence patterns are explained by the characteristics of the plasma components' variations caused by compressive plasma structures. The results indicate that the observed phase-coherence patterns are consistent with the characteristics of fully periodic, realistically composed, and slab turbulence simulations. The correlation between observed and simulated phase-coherence patterns supports the hypothesis that the observed phase-coherence patterns are caused by the characteristics of the plasma components' variations caused by slab-like structures in the plasma. The observed and simulated phase-coherence patterns are explained by the characteristics of the plasma components' variations caused by the plasma structures in the plasma. The results indicate that the observed phase-coherence patterns are consistent with the characteristics of the plasma components' variations caused by the plasma structures in the plasma. In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically around 10s of fs to low 100s of fs in hard X-rays. However, using optical seeding and amplification, we demonstrate a method to bypass this limitation, achieving sub-fs microbunch coherence time compensation. Achieving this, we employ a high-repetition-rate driver laser that delivers pulses within sub-fs temporal uncertainty, coupled with X-ray FEL operations at the LCLS operating at 14.4 keV and a 3 nm energy bandwidth, yielding a predicted coherence time under 1 fs.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are applied to solve this modified equation, yielding an analytical solution that is then compared with the solution for the original equation when viscosity factors are equal.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and
allowed for the identification of biased districting plans.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates gabor filters and histogram of oriented gradients to accurately identify defects while minimizing false positives. A directional gabor filter is applied to fabric images and a specific direction is extracted to create a rich representation suitable for convolutional neural networks. A direction-specific GHOG descriptor is extracted and used with a CNN to classify defects. Furthermore, an adaptive threshold-based inspection method is developed to set the default decision threshold for each fabric image, optimizing the CNN's performance. This method is validated on four fabric types and achieves superior defect detection results, outperforming existing methods, and is presented in this study, including a comprehensive analysis and a publicly available dataset.

Target-driven visual navigation using deep reinforcement learning (DL) is becoming increasingly popular, but it faces challenges related to its inability to adapt to new, unseen environments. To address this issue, we propose an attention-based reinforcement learning (AR) method that leverages the strengths of both attention-based and DL approaches. Specifically, we integrate an attention mechanism within the RL framework to improve handling of uncertain and unseen environments. Experimental evaluations on a standard semi-supervised navigation benchmark demonstrate that our AR model outperforms the baseline DL approach by 10.4% and exhibits improved sample efficiency and generalization to new environments.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. The same analysis applied to photons generates analogous results consistent with the principles of geometric optics.

We examine the potential for the merger of fused Population III binaries within
galactic nuclei and the resulting gravitational wave emissions. Utilizing a
modified version of the open-source code GRWf, which incorporates the physics of
Population III binary remnants, we simulate the evolution of an exponential
disk from the Population III epoch to the present day. Our analysis reveals that
approximately 7% of these remnants will merge during the predicted formation of
nuclear star clusters, producing a gravitational wave signal detectable by
LISA for up to 100 million years before final merger. Additionally, approximately
0.4% of these objects will be captured by supermassive black holes. The
accumulation of these fused remnants in galactic nuclei may potentially alter
the age distribution of stellar clusters in the predicted formation of
galaxies, with approximately one in five Population III binaries falling into
this category.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical components in microgrids that experience faults. Our approach relies on the analysis of smart meter data during events but does not require pre-defined rules or systems. It also focuses on pinpointing the component where the event started and identifies areas impacted by the disturbance. This technique has the potential to be used in conjunction with traditional protection systems and can be applied to locate the source of disturbances such as malfunctions or intentional acts. A detailed simulation based on the69-bus distribution system is carried out to test the effectiveness of this method.

Our study focuses on how the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons contribute to the radiative decays $X(3872) \to J/\psi \pi \gamma$. The investigation begins by examining the experimental observations of these decays and proceeds by analyzing the influence of $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons on $X(3872) \to J/\psi \pi \pi$ and $X(3872) \to J/\psi \pi \gamma$, respectively. The $X(3872) \to J/\psi \pi \pi$ decay is found to be primarily driven by the decay $X(3872) \to \rho^0/J/\psi \pi$, which subsequently decays to $\rho^0 \to \pi \pi$. In the $X(3872) \to J/\psi \gamma$ decay, both the direct and indirect ($X(3872) \to \omega/J/\psi \gamma$) contributions from the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons are considered. The two-body decay widths of the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons are utilized to estimate the magnitude of the $\rho$ and $\omega$ components within the $X(3872) \to J/\psi \gamma$ process. We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform for developing natural language processing skills in AI, requiring the creation of virtual agents capable of invoking complex tools and navigating subtle social nuances. However, the abundance of existing text-based games poses a problem, as agents trained on one game often cannot successfully interact with another due to significant differences in social conventions, inventory, and speech patterns. To address this issue, our study identifies and categorizes the essential skills required for text-based game interaction, including social conventions, inventory management, and language, before evaluating the extent to which existing text-based game subsets contribute to each skill. We discover that interaction with any individual game does not guarantee transferability to other games, but agents trained on multiple, diverse games do exhibit improved transferability. Consequently, we provide concrete guidance for tuning virtual agents to effectively master text-based game interactions.

The interaction between Topological Insulators and crystal dislocations has not been thoroughly investigated to date. This study explores the behavior of Spinless Quantum Hall Conduction in an electron gas on a Topological Insulator's surface influenced by a straight dislocation. A classical approach model is developed to calculate the electron wave function, revealing that the electron density around the dislocation leads to the emergence of a local peak in electron density. Under specific conditions, this local peak corresponds to zero-mode states with well-defined energies, resulting in a minimum in electron density. These findings are supported by First Principles calculations, indicating that the dislocation's core acts as a quantum spin channel with well-defined spin. Additionally, it has been found that increasing the electron gas's Fermi energy results in the disappearance of the local peak in electron density.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model for extreme values, the relationship between wind speed and wave heights in the North East Atlantic is examined. A bivariate Gaussian model is used to examine the extremal dependence of wind speeds and wave heights, with the parameters estimated by combining wind and wave data from 25 stations in the area. The parameters are then used to create simulations of wind speeds and wave heights at multiple locations, revealing the presence of spatial dependence among the 25 locations. These simulations allow for a deeper understanding of the extremal dependence of wind speeds and wave heights across the North East Atlantic.

Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism sets from one variety to another, given that both are defined over a specific number field. Notably, the proof for this result relies on the existing knowledge of Faltings's theorems about the finiteness of maps over the fields of a specific number, given the maps to another fixed target are fixed. In the process, we also revisit the proof of the original Theorem I from Arakelov geometry, reinterpreting it in this context.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human-like motion information, making it useful for teaching and controlling robots in various environments with obstacles and terrain variations. However, extracting this information from human motion data is a challenging task due to the need for a precise 3D motion-capture setup and capturing the whole body movement of the human teacher. In an effort to simplify this process, an online algorithm has been developed to real-time extract manipulability ellipsoids from the motion of a human teacher moving a robot arm in an unencumbered space. The proposed algorithm is easily implementable on robots equipped with depth sensors, like the Kinect, enabling its application in a wide variety of settings. Experimental results from the demonstration on a robot with a depth sensor have been presented to validate the accuracy of the approach.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine the 13 TeV data from the ATLAS and CMS experiments. This technique offers enhanced discrimination between Higgs boson pair and single boson signals, and allows for exploration of various new physics scenarios beyond the Standard Model. We compare the findings of this analysis with existing experimental and theoretical resolutions, and discuss its potential use in future applications.

A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing in-the-wild videos. This approach leverages the diverse perspectives and numerous instances of 3D objects present in such footage, which significantly outnumbers the available images and videos aligned with pose poses. A sequence-based method is developed to extract these perspectives, which are then utilized in a novel single-view 3D object pose estimation framework. This new method effectively reduces the challenge and has shown promising results in three-object classes. Notably, it outperforms the current state-of-the-art by a substantial margin when testing on the 3DPose-WS dataset consisting of threeD object classes, while also demonstrating a substantial five-class performance advantage.

Despite widespread vaccination, a significant number of people remain unvaccinated, which has prompted the disinformation about COVID-19 vaccines to spread rapidly. In our study, we examined how fake news about vaccines performed compared to truthful information on X (formerly Twitter) using three datasets from 2021. We found a link between the volume of disinformation and unvaccination rates in U.S. states. Furthermore, we analyzed how various types of misinformation affected vaccine hesitacy and discovered that not all types of misinformation have the same level of impact. We also determined that unvaccinated individuals were more involved in disseminating misinformation than both hesitant and vaccinated individuals. Finally, we uncovered a distinct pattern of misinformation sharing among different types of vaccinated individuals.

Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential, particularly in attaining higher macroscopic conversion yields from higher-order harmonic sources and achieving higher driving laser intensities without ionization interference. Developing attosecond pulses with enhanced brightness and temporal precision is critical. Intensities of the main pulse of the driver laser can be reduced by leveraging the self-steepening effect caused by the optical phase shift accumulated by the intense pulse as it propagates through a gas, resulting in a more intense and shorter pulse at the trailing edge. This effect also prevents the main pulse from overlapping with the main pulse of the driver, thus minimizing ionization. A few-optowatt attosecond pulse generator based on the trailing edge of a more intense and shorter self-steepened laser pulse has been proposed and demonstrated by numerically simulating the parameters. These simulations predict a far-field attosecond pulse yield in excess of 100 microjoules per pulse with a feasibility rate of at least 10 percent, thus potentially revolutionizing experiments involving extremely weak phenomena due to its high brightness.

Eclipse predictions for binary stars can be made with high accuracy, and any deviations from this forecast can offer insights into the properties of these binaries. Observations of changes in eclipse timing can be used to detect periodic variations caused by the presence of a third body, often resulting in the formation of triply eclipsing systems. In this research, we analyze the eclipse timings of 39 different binary and triple binary systems from the COR-BIN and later time catalogs to verify our predictions and understand any periodic changes that may occur. Our findings for several systems agree with previous studies, and for a few systems where no prior study existed, we have discovered new triple systems and determined their orbital characteristics, including those of 2020a+2020b whose existence was first suggested in this study.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation with initial conditions in the space $H^1$, under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity $|u|^{p-1}u$ and negative energy. It is observed that solutions become unbounded in a finite time for those initial conditions where the energy is greater than zero, and also becomes unbounded in a finite time when the energy is zero, provided the $L^{10}$-norm of the initial condition exceeds a certain threshold. The results of this study extend and generalise an earlier finding made by Yang in 2019.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving impressive results on single- and multi-scale problems, their ability to address these issues consistently remains partial. A particular case study involves the numerical approximation of a parametrized family of PDEs, for which our approach leverages both the full solution set and sample points to train the full solution. A comparison of our approach with alternative strategies shows significant improvements in prediction accuracy and sample efficiency. Additionally, our network is equipped with a built-in differential operator, eliminating the need for costly and often infeasible training and testing evaluations.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by analyzing the oscillations in their electrostatic conduction band profile. We have modelled the negative capacitance effect in ferroelectric transistors, which can be attributed to the soft mode within these devices. Our analysis also takes into consideration the size of the domain wall, which may vary in the ferroelectric layer. The study demonstrates that negative capacitance is a viable option for the source region of a transistor, but not the drain, due to variations in the electric field. We have also analyzed the impact of drain voltage on the domain size and found that a higher voltage leads to domain shrinkage, making the source region's domain shrinkage faster than the drain's. We have also observed that the domain wall size remains unaffected by changes in gate voltage, while the leakage current of a ferroelectric transistor is dependent on both the domain wall size and size of the non-ferroelectric channel.

A significant knowledge gap exists in the field of Software Engineering concerning cargo-related security issues, necessitating comprehensive research in this area. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical investigation into cargo security vulnerabilities, revealing that cargo, its subcomponents like crate, package, and library, constitute the primary focus of the Cargo Rust Ecosystem (CRE). Our analysis, based on data from 2007 to 2022, showed that security vulnerabilities are the most prevalent type of CRE issue, with information disclosure being the most severe data security risk. We further identified the open-source security community, CVE, and CVE ID as the external sources most influential on CVEs in CRE. Circular dependency, identified as the most severe data integrity risk, is significantly influenced by external factors, with GitHub, CVE ID, and the open-source security community playing crucial roles.

For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to demonstrate irreducibility. This paper confirms the irreducibility of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subjected to discrete jump noises and shows that these results facilitate the examination of ergodic properties in such equations. Discrepancies in the approaches for discrete jump noises and countably many noises are also examined.

For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing the minimal vertex degree in its power graph. This power graph connects vertices based on one being a positive power of the other. By examining the group's prime divisors and Sylow subgroups, we've pinpointed vertices related to its cyclic subgroups. This allows us to establish a connection between the group's properties and its minimal vertex degree in the power graph. This study provides degree calculations for specific types of noncyclic abelian groups.

Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been extensively studied at high-energy ranges above sqrt(s) = 63 GeV using the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings. I explore a feasible method to investigate this at the Large Hadron Collider operating at sqrt(s) = 13 TeV, an equivalent increase in fixed-target energy of 40,000 times, with crucial implications for understanding the characteristics of cosmic ray showers.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), have achieved impressive results in image recognition but also introduced a high computational barrier. This has also led to DCNNs being largely inapplicable for real-time image processing on resource-limited devices. This paper presents OCNs (Orientation Convolution Networks), which overcome these limitations by (1) speeding up model training and inference speeds, (2) lowering the computational load, and (3) enhancing recognition accuracy. OCNs reimagines the process of image feature extraction by employing oriented filters and a novel fully convularized feature aggregation network. Experimental results on three benchmark datasets confirm the efficacy of our proposed OCNs in terms of both speed and accuracy.

This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks when applied to point clouds. By employing Computation Graph Optimization (CGO) to eliminate redundant nodes and edges, we successfully reduced model memory requirements, which in turn allowed us to design a novel, lightweight graph convolutional network called Lightweight Graph Convolution. This novel building block consists of two streamlined layers that maintain high performance while significantly improving efficiency. Using this graph convolutional network, we achieved state-of-the-art results on a range of 3D semantic segmentation and semantic segmentation semantic labeling tasks, including SCENNET, SUN-RCB, KITTI and SceneNet UNPO.
