u]^\mathcal{F}$ spatial symmetry and $N$-particle number, where $
u$ represents the orbital angular momentum and $N$ is the number of particles. This efficient storage method enables precise calculations of atomic nuclei incorporating three-nucleon forces up to a high maximum orbital angular momentum $l_{max}=18$. Using this approach, we have successfully obtained three-nucleon matrix elements involving the $d$-wave and performed full no-core shell model computations incorporating these interactions in the $^{12}$C nucleus. Furthermore, we have examined the impact of the $E_{3max}$ limitation on the point-convergence with $N$ and $n$ in the computation of the $^{12}$C $d$-root mean square radius, and found that it significantly influences the predictions derived from three-nucleon forces.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases. To achieve this, we will employ widely accessible techniques, including tight-binding models and wavefunction methods. The Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model will serve as our primary example to demonstrate how to compute topological invariants and explore the effects of disordered systems. Building upon this foundation, additional topics such as higher-order topological phases, the fractional quantum Hall effect, and quantum computing will be covered, all using introductory concepts. We will also explain the significance of these topics for quantum computer science.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ and USp(4) and found it to be consistent with a two-loop Witten diagram result, also confirming the amplitude's conformal symmetry. This supported the hypothesis that gravitational amplitudes in AdS space can be represented by finite combinations of logarithmic zigzag integrals. Although the amplitude contains divergent zigzag integrals in flat space time, it can still be used to compute the corresponding flat space amplitude through appropriate regularization and limiting procedures. However, such a process does not directly yield the flat space amplitude due to additional contact terms resulting from the limit process, which may also explain related issues in celestial amplitudes.

High-performance computing is gaining prominence in scientific discovery and is gaining prominence in educational institutions. To advance the field of HPC, the Science of Programming needs to progress to the level of HPC's complexities. To address the challenge of making complex HPC algorithms understandable and teachable, the HPC-Design Language was created. HPC-Design is innovative for its simple invariants that facilitate the development of robust HPC algorithms. This work presents HPC-Design's novel features along with a functional case study that demonstrates their effectiveness. Specifically, the case study focuses on Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO) design pattern in HPC. The successful implementation of the SMMO pattern is illustrated through the development of a vector-sum vectorization approach that achieves high levels of hardware parallelism using the COBAYA2 probabilistic vectorization tool.

We introduce family universal U(1)X models incorporating three right-handed neutrinos, by defining U(1)X as a composite of SO(10) U(1)Y and U(1)χ gauge symmetries. To incorporate quantum gravity effects, we propose the introduction of a Dirac fermion dark matter candidate that is odd under Z2 symmetry linked to the proton stability, while also being incompatible with neutrino oscillations. Within these models, we can achieve the correct hot dark matter fraction of neutrinos at the present time, which is consistent with observational data, through the simultaneous emergence of a IR-fugitive U(1)X gauge force and the seesaw mechanism's contribution to neutrino masses.

A specific measurement technique for assessing the mechanical characteristics of straw tubes is described, which uses the knowledge of tube wall thickness to calculate Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio. These two properties are critical in determining the stable operational voltage and the effective length of the straw tubes. By measuring the longitudinal breakdown voltage of multiple straw tubes, a statistical analysis of their strength is conducted, and a method for improving their mechanical properties is identified.

In various fields, including machine learning and statistics, there is a growing interest in quantifying the uncertainty of decision functions. To achieve this, researchers have developed measures of decision risk uncertainty. A particular type of risk uncertainty measure, known as marginal risk uncertainty, can be optimized to find an upper bound. This optimization process involves solving the maximum marginal probability (MARmax) problem. Unfortunately, the original MARmax problem is computationally challenging, and existing solutions often fail to consider the structure of decision risk functions. To address this limitation, we introduce a new, simplified MARmax problem for linkers - widely used logit-based risk functions. Our proposed method outperforms previous solutions in efficiency and provides an accurate estimate for the maximum marginal probability.

In a supersolid Bose-Einstein condensate with a spin-orbit coupling, an accelerated impurity atom exhibits oscillations that mirror Bloch oscillations in solid matter, despite causing condensate excitements that give rise to internal phonon modes. However, these oscillations have no impact on the condensate's roton minimum position, thereby preserving its periodic matter wave pattern. Notably, the oscillations fade away when the superfluid phase is adopted, and they also have significant implications for understanding how accelerated impurities behave in superfluids and superfluids.

In a generalised quadrangle, a code is a subset of the vertices in the quadrangle's point-set $\mathbb{F}_q^4$, where $\mathbb{F}_q$ is a finite field. The distance between two points $x$ and $y$ in the quadrangle is defined as the number of indices $i$ for which $x_i$ is not equal to $y_i$. A code is considered a $(s, r, w, \ell)$-code if it has a minimum distance of 4 and the coordinates of the code's codewords satisfy $0 \le x_1 < s$, $0 \le x_2 < r$, $0 \le x_3 < w$, and $0 \le x_4 < \ell$. The associated code $\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S})$ is defined by a set of lines $\mathcal{S}$ in the quadrangle, where the coordinates of the code's codewords are determined by the $i$-th line's intersection with the quadrangle's $i$-th axis. The associated code $\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S})$ is equidistant, meaning that for any two lines $i$ and $j$ in the quadrangle, the distance between them is the same. The main goal of this paper is to establish a method for constructing equidistant codes from a set

Located at the very center of the Milky Way, the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) boasts exceptionally high gas densities that are an order of magnitude greater than in the interstellar space of our solar neighborhood. Although the presence of gas in the CMZ is known, its density distribution remains unclear, with hypotheses ranging from uniform to layered structures. To gain insight into the density structure of the CMZ, researchers used the Adler Observatory's multilobe H-alpha telescope to observe the Milky Way's central region at a wavelength of 656 nm. The telescope's design enables the observation of gas at specific velocities relative to the Earth, providing valuable insights into the density distribution of gas within the Milky Way's central region. The results revealed that the gas within the Milky Way's central region is not uniformly distributed but rather exhibits a patchy, non-uniform structure.

To study rapid changes occurring at an extremely fast pace, ultra-fast X-ray techniques utilize an X-ray laser that produces high energy, allowing researchers to examine the time-evolution of material changes. The speed of these induced material changes depends on the energy per area delivered by the X-ray source to the sample, and understanding this relationship is crucial. In this research, we investigate the effect of varying the energy per area delivered by an X-ray laser to a single unit of iron and observe the changes in the X-ray absorption near edge spectrum. By comparing our results to ab initio simulations, we have identified the s-process as the primary mechanism responsible for the observed changes and understanding its implications is essential for interpreting future experiments.

This research presents the development and testing of a temperature sensor in CMOS, incorporated within a system featuring dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS). The goal of this work falls within the broader context of creating intelligent, self-adjusting CMOS circuits capable of adapting to adaptive CMOS techniques and self-heating phenomena. Previous studies highlighted the need for precise temperature monitoring in devices utilizing the DVFS method and reported difficulties in measuring large voltage drops. Our innovation utilizes a temperature-dependent reverse-biased PN-junction, offering an advantageous benefit due to its operation on minuscule power requirements. Moreover, our sensor exhibits a notable shift in bandgap temperature ranging between $2 mV/K$ and $-0.002mV/K$, influenced by the reverse bias current, with these parameters directly impacting the linear temperature dependence of the generated signal. Ultimately, our design facilitates temperature determination through the measurement of the background current in the junction, offering an efficient and reliable monitoring solution.

Quantum entanglement plays a vital role in quantum information sciences and technologies. Among various forms of entanglement, polarization entanglement is the most prevalent. To better understand and improve existing technologies, we will begin by examining the concept of entanglement and its significance before exploring the various methods used to generate polarization entanglement among the D-dimensional photonic states. Furthermore, we will examine the ability to analyze entangled states using entropy measures, with further examples of model applications also being considered.

This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. Initially, the authors establish a lower bound of Ω(ε^(-1)log n / log d) on the competitive ratio for any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm for points in 1-dimension, proving it to be tight when d equals 1. For scenarios where d exceeds 1, the authors show that the lower bound can be improved to Ω(ε^(-1)d). Building on this, the authors prove the existence of an online (1+ε)-t-spanner algorithm with a competitive ratio of O(t^2ε^(-1)d+1) for any integer t greater than or equal to 1, which represents the first known upper bound for graphs of arbitrary constant orderliness in the online geometric setting. Furthermore, the authors provide near-matching lower and upper bounds for scenarios where the points are given in d dimensions, demonstrating that online t-spanner algorithms have inherent geometric complexities. It is worth noting that equivalent results are not feasible for offline t-spanner algorithms, which highlight the unique challenges posed by the online geometric setting. Ultimately, this work lays the groundwork for further exploration of other offline algorithms in the online geometric context.

Identifying IoT devices is a vital task for network security, but classifying IoT devices via MAC addresses is impractical due to the network performance costs associated with the required feature extraction. To address this challenge, we introduce MacNet, a neural network model that uses the names provided by the device as inputs, combined with multi-task learning to enhance performance and reduce computational costs. We compare MacNet to other deep learning models, including those using recurrent and convolutional neural networks, as well as a bag-of-words approach, and demonstrate that MacNet achieves better performance with lower computational costs.

This study provides an introduction to G\"odel modal logics, which combine intuitionistic logic with different modalities, including truth definitions. Unlike traditional intuitionistic modal logics, G\"odel modal logics allow for the inclusion of a "true if and only if" definition without resulting in inconsistent systems. Although the concept was initially proposed by D. Skvortsova, it has received little attention compared to analogous concepts for classical logic. These logics offer a framework in which the semantics and correspondences between various G\"odel modal languages can be thoroughly investigated.

This research presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on a relatively small dataset. Furthermore, in terms of alignment accuracy, our approach outperforms GIZA++ when utilizing external bilingual information.

We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they could potentially be discovered through gravitational waves produced by oscillating spacetime structures known as cosmic strings, which might form at the points where PBHs split in the early universe. We examine the dark matter scenario in which early universe dark matter is composed of such fluctuating structures rather than PBHs, and investigate the potential for cosmic string-induced gravitational waves to explain recent scientific findings, including the GW190817 event and the anomaly in the cosmic microwave background spectrum, as well as data from the Lyman-alpha forest.

We investigated the liquid crystalline behavior of uniform, wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations. These molecules feature a single axis of symmetry and variable wedge angles. At low packing densities, below 0.5, only a single liquid crystalline phase was observed, regardless of the wedge angle. This phase exhibited nematic characteristics and was identified as a combination of parallel head-to-tail and perpendicular alignments of the molecules. However, at packing densities of 0.5 and above, an additional smectic A liquid crystalline phase emerged at wedge angles of 60 or 90 degrees. This same condition triggered a blue phase in molecules with a 90-degree wedge angle.

Recurrence relations exist among the coefficients of certain zonal functions on the unit sphere, linked to expansions in Gegenbauer polynomials. We derive these relations and examine how they impact the positivity of these functions. Furthermore, we explore the implications for positive functions on the sphere that can be expressed as infinite sums of Gegenbauer polynomials with non-decreasing coefficients, specifically in relation to their restrictions to great circles.

A typical imaging scenario necessitates three essential elements: (1) light source, (2) specimen, and (3) detector. Traditionally, this light source-specimen-detector setup operates with fixed positions, restricting innovations to alterations in these components or their positioning. Breaking this paradigm, researchers have devised an imaging system featuring three moving parts - (1) a rotating LED array light source, (2) a translating stage specimen holder, and (3) a rotating detector array - to enable unique, synchronized imaging, stimulated by concepts from single-pixel imaging and incoherent computed tomography. The breakthrough lies in integrating these three mobility sources to enable diverse synchronized imaging configurations, incoherently capturing 2D data, and reconstructing coherent 2D images, cross-sectional data, and 3D objects, all while employing standard imaging equipment.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combination of experimental and numerical studies on model liquids. namely tar and water, over various synthetic surfaces. we have shown that the liquid's outflow rate as a function of applied pressure exhibits three distinct friction regimes. These regimes correspond to the presence or absence of trapped air pockets within the surface structure's voids. The occurrence of trapped air is determined by a hierarchy of time scales, specifically the trap residence times, the liquid's characteristic viscoelastic time, and the hydrodynamic escape times. The possibility of a "frictionless" slip regime, free of trapped air, is contingent on the availability of an intermediate roughness in the surface structure, with a range that is not present in most naturally occurring surfaces.

This report details our method that secured a top position in the 2019 ISIC competition through collaboration with Universite' du Quebec a Chicoutimi and Universite' du Quebec a Trois-Rivieres. Our winning strategy involved utilizing the Keras framework, paired with an in-house implemented stochastic depth technique and an in-house developed two-branch asymmetric FPN framework. Additionally, we outlined a simplified version of the framework that can be easily adapted using TensorFlow or PyTorch.

We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from earlier research. These findings amplify the need for theoretical models more advanced than the random phase approximation. Contrary to the hypothesis that mass enhancement is limited due to the short lifespan of electrons, our results show that the effects of lifetime limitations are minimal.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible transformations. We present two solutions to overcome this obstacle, each producing distinct results for the heat and work exchanged between the system and its surroundings. One solution, derived from a specific final microstate, yields finite values for the transferred energy. In contrast, the solution that incorporates the probability distribution of the resulting microstates aligns with the traditional thermodynamic expectations, showing a significant deviation from it only at the microscopic level. Additionally, we found that the work done within the system during free expansion is not inherently non-negative,而是can take on negative values, which can be attributed to the system's inherent fluctuations.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate how curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined through a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression that combines it with a formula for the underlying connection graph weights. Notably, we examine a cotangent bundle case, leading to a substantial simplification of the curvature expression.

We explore the phenomenon of nanoptera its occurrence in a specific type of wave equation known as the SGPHEWEP. This phenomenon originally appeared in the context of singularly perturbed harmonic chains but was found to persist in the newly developed model. Our research reveals that the phenomenon in this new model arises from two distinct mechanisms. These mechanisms are interconnected local and global interactions. These interactions combine to produce the observed exponential decay. This decay in turn leads to the observed plateau.

Extra energy injected into our universe during inflation could be responsible for
various phenomena like reheat anisotropy and suppression of large-scale structure.
In this study, we investigate the behavior of a cosmological model featuring
classical oscillations that transport this extra energy between their era and the
domination of background inflation. We show that the cosmological perturbation
equations can be solved analytically for both the scalar and tensor components by
transforming the equations into a system with constant coefficients. This
constitutes a comprehensive and comprehensive framework for the cosmological
perturbation equations, enabling the infinite cospectrum of modes to be determined
for all perturbation types. We demonstrate that the perturbation solutions maintain
their amplitude during the transition from their constant coefficients in the
oscillating domain to the exponentially decaying solutions characteristic of the
exponentially expanding domain. We further show that the solutions satisfy the
five cosmodes of modes, with the mode of invariants of the perturbation solutions
preserved across the transition of domains. We explore the boundary condition
that links the perturbation solutions between the two domains and find that the
boundary condition is independent of the parameter of the cospectrum. This
constitutes a comprehensive framework for the cosmological perturbation equations,
enabling a comprehensive understanding of the cosmological perturbation equations,
along with the associated cosmodes of modes.

Consider a graph of even order G and its complete graph counterpart K_G. A pairing of G refers to a perfect matching of K_G. A graph has the PH-property if for each pairing of K_G, there exists a Hamiltonian path of the graph. Cubic graphs are examples of graphs with the PH-property, but the property is limited to this class. In contrast, 3-connected bipartite graphs do not share this property, which prompts the exploration of the property's constraints. This study classifies the largest groups of graphs by inclusion that exhibit the PH-property.

We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis in a three-state quantum walk. The coin operator is represented by a symmetric tridiagonal matrix with parameters similar to a specific quantum walk model. The system's dynamics depend on the mixing angle θ. As θ approaches 0, the middle state's influence diminishes, effectively reducing the system to a two-state quantum walk. The wavepacket's spreading speed is higher in the three-state model compared to the standard two-state Goyette model. The system's dynamics can be likened to a form of quantum erasure, where varying θ alters the outcomes.

This paper explores the benefits of self-supervised learning when applied to Vision Transformer architectures. Specifically, it addresses semantic segmentation tasks by comparing supervised and self-supervised approaches to Vision Transformers, as well as examining the impact of patch-based transformer architecture, pre-training strategies, and the use of convolutional patch-based frequency-domain masking. Furthermore, the study trained and evaluated multiple models on the Cityscapes dataset using various training techniques and compared them to existing semantic segmentation benchmarks. Our research reveals that self-supervised learning is highly competitive with supervised learning in semantic segmentation. Both models demonstrate similar state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes dataset's easy and difficult evaluation criteria. Our analysis also provides insight into the design and assessment of vision transformers. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/aspathy/Unsupervised_RangeFormer.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines dissipative and phantom fluid,
resulting in a more efficient and flexible framework for understanding the current phase of the universe.
By using the ansatz of the dissipative and phantom fluid, the authors derive the dissipative density,
dissipative pressure, equation of state parameter for the dark fluid, and the entropy density of the dark fluid.
The study then employs the f(T) Bogoslovsky and Ferraro-Ib\'{a}\~{n}ez models as the faring matter sectors
and utilizes the Hubble data set, cosmic chronometer data, and the PHENOM-JLA equation of state parameter,
resulting in the best-fit parameters and further analysis of the models.
The most favorable fit is found in the f(T) Bogoslovsky model with dissipative density,
while the most favorable fit with dissipative pressure is found in the f(T) Ferraro-Ib\'{a}\~{n}ez model.
The research then examines the behavior of the equation of state parameter and finds that
with dissipative pressure, it crosses the phantom barrier in the FFI model,
whereas with dissipative density, it only does so in the FTB model.
The study also investigates the nature of the dark fluid by analyzing entropy density,
finding that with dissipative density, it remains positive in the FTB and FI models with a decreasing trend

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have achieved significant success, but directly editing images via image-prompt text is a challenging task. To address this challenge, SeGa (Semantic Guidance) was developed to learn a semantic space in which images can be encoded and manipulated based on text descriptions. SEGA's first step involves encoding an original image and extracting low-frequency components, then training a semantic space where original image embeddings are clustered, and manipulating images by editing other image embeddings with the text. However, this approach has a major limitation, since image SEGA encoding still relies heavily on high-frequency components and local pixel information, thus resulting in blurry generated images and requiring multiple tries to achieve the desired editing. A significant breakthrough was made by High-frequency Guidance (HiGa), an SEGA extension that extracts and preserves high-frequency components in the original image and incorporates them into the base image SEGA encoding, thus preserving both low and high-frequency information in the original image. HiGa enables high-fidelity SEGA base image generation and complex editing, and demonstrates superior performance over other SEGA approaches in T2I generation, image editing, and hallucination tasks.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible chemistry. However, an implicit trust in these models is reinforced by their exceptional performance on chemistry datasets, overlooking the uncertainties they might be introducing. By training deep neural networks using Bayesian deep learning techniques, we can extract both aleatoric and non-aleatoric uncertainties from the trained models, thereby distinguishing between random noise and systematic uncertainty. When combined with ensemble methods, this approach yields highly accurate predictions for various properties of molecules, including their ground and excited states, as well as efficient light absorption, while also providing reliable uncertainty estimates, an essential component often neglected in standard deep learning models.

Our study investigates the light neutrino sector using particle physics, with a particular focus on the $J/\psi$ particle's invisible decay. In a recent examination by $LMB$ at Koeln, a significant signal of the $J/\psi$ decaying into invisible particles was identified in events involving $\psi(2S)$ and other $D$ meson spallation processes. These results imply interesting connections to the existence of light sterile neutrinos, a particular mass model in which the active neutrinos are composed of four or more mass eigenstates, and where the heavier neutrinos decay into lighter neutrinos. In this analysis, we explore the lighter neutrino's decay within the framework of the four-neutrino model in which the $J/\psi$ is produced by a neutrino and an anti-neutrino, which then decay into a lepton and a $Z$ boson. This study is then expanded to encompass the full spectrum of lighter neutrino-mass-mixing-parameter spaces and provides constraints for the lighter neutrino's properties.

Magnetic bright points (MBP) in the solar photosphere, observable with high-resolution telescopes, serve as key reference points for studying the solar surface, given their widespread presence, despite being relatively small in area. This study, based on images from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, focused on identifying these MBUT through a machine learning algorithm and analyzing their spatial distribution, size, and intensity. By employing this approach, we identified 1,111 MBUT and discovered that their area and diameter follow a lognormal pattern, while their overall brightness follows a mixed distribution, consisting of two or three normal components. MBUT are evenly spread across the observed section of the solar surface, with no evident variation across different latitude or longitude areas. Furthermore, we examined the movement of MBUT and found an average shift of 12.26 ± 1.13 arcseconds over the 12-hour observation period, equating to a speed of approximately 0.125 km/s.

Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or movement data, 
but combining these cues is crucial for low-light or motion blur conditions. 
However, using multiple cameras can compensate for these issues, and our study, 
OCNet, aims to improve recognition in such scenarios by utilizing the information 
from each camera individually, then combining their 'expert' predictions. 
Unlike previous methods, our approach does not require the cameras to be 
identical, and our novel architecture, incorporating a recent development, allows 
it to process the images from each camera separately. 
Our research shows that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, 
especially in low-light or motion blur conditions, and it also performs 
competitively in standard, single-camera settings, according to our visual 
recognition benchmarks, TRECVID and OCIC.

Dark particles magnetic monopoles have an unusual characteristic of being able to pass through ordinary matter without interaction, and they have an equally intriguing property of causing an oscillation in the elliptical shape of celestial halos over time, and this phenomenon could potentially be detected by astronomical observations. These monopoles, which can permeate the Earth and space alike, cease inducing an anomaly in halo ellipses' time-period when their density in the local solar neighborhood decreases, and this decrease is tied to changes in the local radiation pressure they exert on nearby matter, and this decrease, however, results in the formation of clumps and substructures within the local galaxy due to the compression of the dark particles magnetic monopoles, and such an accumulation, although not directly observable, can indirectly influence the movement and velocities of celestial objects and stars near the Earth, and such effects could potentially be mistaken for signs of extra-solar gravitational influence.

Weather forecasting relies on accurate predictions, but traditional weather models are limited by their complexity, preventing deep learning integration. To fill this gap, we developed a Swin-Transformer model for precise weather forecasting, involving 24 hours of single-variable predictions at a 10km spatial resolution and 1-hour temporal resolution. We also compiled a dataset of global atmospheric variables from the ERA5 reanalysis over Europe, involving 7 types of variables and 144 spatial grids. The model was fine-tuned using data from 1 hour to 2 days and achieved a 90% improvement in accuracy, validating our approach as promising for real-world applications.

In models that expand on the scalar sector of the electroweak sector, a viable candidate for dark matter arises from $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetric scalars. We investigate the implications of adding a right-handed neutrino to the K钟$-$Maurer potential dark matter model, specifically looking at the consequences for the baryon number-violating sphaleron process. By analyzing the impact of additional scalar fields on the dark matter-scatter interaction and their influence on the sphaleron, we find that constraints from both dark matter data and baryon number violation can be satisfied, thereby preserving the baryon asymmetry of the universe.

A comprehensive study on the PPT square conjecture is presented with a notable achievement: the PPT square conjecture's validity has been rigorously demonstrated for the case involving finite-dimensional space.

Intracellular transportation is crucial for delivering vital materials to specific cell areas, enabling complex neuronal functions. Disruption of this process is linked to various neurodegenerative diseases, making it essential to understand the molecular mechanisms behind transportation failures. This study presents a unique approach to monitoring fluorescent vesicles in axons, allowing for the evaluation of multiple trafficking parameters. By applying this method to vesicles associated with synaptic proteins and other components, the researchers were able to distinguish between functional and impaired vesicles. The results indicate that a significant portion of vesicles associated with the protein PSD95 in hyper-aged fruit flies are dysfunctional. Furthermore, the study compares the transportation parameters of vesicles containing the proteins Dynactin1 or Dynacin for 2 hours and the intraxonal vesicles in control vs. aged synapses.

Billion-dollar losses inflicted by banking fraud across the globe make graph-based fraud detection in transactions increasingly significant. In analyzing transaction patterns, researchers utilize graphs to identify novel and complex schemes. This research aims to identify real-world transaction network patterns, specifically network motifs within a heterogenous transaction dataset. We also present a method for generating genuine banking transaction graphs via randomization. The outcome of our preliminary analysis indicates that extracting network motifs can reveal meaningful and understandable patterns within the data.

In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine how a white dwarf is shed due to a black hole's tidal forces, resulting in the emission of electromagnetic and gravitational waves. We observe that during this process, the emitted light is primarily of the TUV type, consistent with the ultraviolet output of a standard star. Furthermore, the emitted radiation is polarized, and its spectrum is heightened by hot electrons at temperatures of around 10^7-10^8 K, which are magnetically driven into the cooler gas. We observe that repeated episodes of tidal force can lead to the complete destruction of a star within approximately 100 repetitions, and each episode produces bursts of radiation that last around the time it takes for light to traverse the white dwarf. We note that these bursts of radiation are particularly intense in the X-ray range, where their flux is around 10^3 times the sensitivity of the XMM-Newton satellite. We observe that the X-ray burst from these bursts can be mistaken for an unstable helium flame, particularly when their timescales are the same. We observe that the emitted gravitational waves peak at a frequency that is twice the inverse of the time period, and their amplitude is around 10^-5 at a frequency of around 100 Hz. Finally, we observe that the emitted signals from these bursts can be detected by an LIGO or LISA detector, even without taking into account the effects of the host galaxy's motion, such

Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions with light hadrons and CP symmetry violations, are crucial areas of study in electro-weak physics. The knowledge of hadronic properties in these decays, particularly the form factors of light hadrons, is limited and needs further investigation. Understanding CP violations in three-body leptonic decays can be achieved through analyzing asymmetries with the help of the helicity amplitude method. This research focuses on incorporating the non-resonant background using helicity amplitudes $A_L$, which are influenced by various resonances in the hadronic sector. By breaking down amplitudes into $A_+$ and $A_-$ and applying the subtraction technique, this non-relativistic approach effectively incorporates isospin, and it is demonstrated that such amplitudes are not form-dependent.

This paper focuses on evaluating the properties of four widely used evaluation metrics in set-theoretic frameworks, including Tversky, F-beta, and Tversky-f-beta models. These evaluation measures assess the similarity between two sets by calculating weighted combinations of their intersection and difference. We first establish that both the Tversky and Tversky-f-beta models meet the requirements for a symmetric Tversky-like structure. Subsequently, we determine under what conditions these Tversky-based models can be considered a metric. Additionally, for each of the eight possible E-Measures identified in previous studies, we provide a current popular equivalent and derive their relationship.

A recent breakthrough in motion deblurring technique utilizes data with artificial blur created by convolution. However, this synthetic blur often differs significantly from the real blur due to limitations in current blurring methods. To overcome this issue, we propose a novel, convolution-based synthetic blur method that mimics the point spread function (PSF) more accurately. By matching the PSF distribution, our proposed method enables the deep learning-based deblurring algorithm to achieve better results near object edges. Moreover, we demonstrate that using our synthetic blur data leads to superior deblurring performance compared to using real blurry images for training, as evaluated through the standard degradation pipeline.

Hebbian learning, capable of functioning with only local access to pre- and post-synaptic signals, enables autonomous learning through an adjustability rule that increases the strength of the connection between two neurons when they are active simultaneously. As a widespread form of early brain learning, it is also observed in both biological neurons and artificial neurons. This article explores the application of Hebbian learning in both biological neurons and artificial neurons.

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill the open completeness property in the ultrapower. To achieve open completeness in the ultrapower, an underlying set with the same property and a specific mapping rule can be used. Although open completeness cannot be guaranteed for all sets, using the properties of complete sets can help achieve this in many real-world applications like theoretical computer science.

Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science rely on accurately computing and modeling complex phenomena, which is essential for the many real-world problems that require the use of massive scientific datasets. However, these datasets are often complex and noisy, presenting significant challenges in computational capabilities. As a result, these limitations necessitate the comparison of different computational models to ensure reliable results. One effective approach to model assessment is through metrics and benchmarks that measure model performance, but their effectiveness is often limited by their sensitivity to dataset-specific characteristics. In this study, an advanced framework for comparing datasets and models is proposed, which can automate the evaluation of dataset similarity and model accuracy, while also considering dataset properties. Furthermore, this framework is being applied to assess the performance of different computational models across diverse datasets, thus providing insight into the degree of dataset representativeness and the impact of dataset characteristics on model rankings.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph with t vertices. This has been reinforced by another theory suggesting such a substructure, known as a topological minor, should exist. In this research, we further strengthen this by showing that this type of complete graph, without any additional connections, exists within any multicoloring with list colors where each vertex has a specific set of allowed colors with a specific size. Hadwiger's and Thompson's conjectures are actually specific instances of our main findings, corresponding to eight and nine-colored graphs, respectively.

This research introduces an advanced algorithm for efficiently recovering smooth graph signals through generalized graph deconvolution, Generalized Correlation Regression (GCR). We reformulate the problem of minimizing the weighted mean squared error as a linear system of equations and employ an adaptive, iterative algorithm to solve it. This algorithm is characterized by a finite representation and does not necessitate the precise determination of kernel width. Furthermore, it exhibits convergence to the global optimum under a broad and general condition. Our simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm, Generalized Correlation Regression (GCR), outperforms existing methods and does not require an accurate estimate of the kernel width.

Theoretical investigations are conducted to design and control entangled atomic states formed through spin-changing collisions within a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate for use in a more robust atom interferometry capable of withstanding common technical problems like detector limitations. It is discovered through both analytical and numerical examinations of the spin-changing collision process that utilizing a small initial disturbance as a trigger, as opposed to vacuum fluctuations, can offer benefits in terms of efficiency and consistency under certain conditions. Our findings are anticipated to contribute to the development of more efficient and reliable entangled atomic state producers for application in more precise entangled atom interferometry.

The purpose of this research paper is to derive optimal estimates for the first eigenvalue of the first Robin eigenvalue problem involving the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator. This problem seeks to minimize a specific functional over all nonzero functions in the Sobolev space, and involves several variables and constants, including $p$, a bounded mean convex domain $\Omega$ in $N$-dimensional space, and a smooth norm $F$ on this space.

Deep Neural Networks have gained significant attention in recent years due to their diverse applications and capabilities. A variation of this technology, the Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GCNN), is becoming increasingly popular in systems that process graph-structured data. Despite the success of standard neural networks in many fields, GCNNs still face limitations in learning efficient feature extractors through their convolution layers. These layers, which generalize the concept of pixel interaction in image processing, are crucial in most existing graph-based systems but lack a unified definition and rigorous foundation. This document seeks to address this issue by providing a systematic study and analysis of convolution layers on graphs.

A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages. However, its effectiveness heavily relies on access to comprehensive, annotated data for each target language - a resource that is not always available. To address this limitation, we propose a novel self-training technique that enables models to enhance their own performance by leveraging both existing labeled data and unannotated sentences from the same or a different language. Unlike traditional methods that rely on a fixed set of rules, our technique integrates knowledge from morphological and contextual word representations, allowing it to more effectively apply what it knows to previously unprocessed sentences. Our approach demonstrates significant gains in parsing accuracy for low-resource languages including Turkish, Czech, and German, as well as remarkable generalization capabilities to unseen languages such as Turkish and Greek.

We've investigated the transition form factors $f_+(q^2)$ and $f_-(q^2)$ for the $Bightarrow D\ell
u$ semileptonic decay process, considering both the light front quark model and the equation of motion of quark fields. Our analysis also involved calculating the total width $\Gamma_{bightarrow d\ell
u}$ and the coupling matrix $K$. These calculations enabled us to determine the differential branching ratio $\mathcal{B}(x)$ and the integrated branching fraction $\mathcal{B}(bightarrow d\ell
u)$ for the $B_{u(s)}ightarrow D_{u(s)}\ell
u$ $B$-meson decays. The results for $B_{u(s)}ightarrow D_{u(s)}\ell
u$ $B$-meson decays are then compared with experimental findings.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

In continuous logic, CPT-formulas can be thought of as an infinite version of first-order formulas from classical logic, CPT stands for continuous first-order predicate logic. The terms "CPT-definable" and "$\mathcal{C}$-def" are used to describe properties that can be captured by CPT-formulas and continuous first-order formulas, respectively. Our work examines two specific properties: query definability of the CFI-query and the $\mathcal{C}$-definability of 2-coloring with respect to connected components. The CFI-query is a query that is not CPT-definable on the class of all graphs, but is definable according to the Erdős-Spencer theorem. The property of being 2-colorable with respect to connected components is not CPT-definable on the class of all colourings, but is definable according to the Giraudet theorem. Our results show that these properties are not definable within the continuous framework, but may still be effective in classical terms. The theorem of Giraudet is actually a particular case of our more general result. Our work also relates to a broader question raised by Baelde and Montanari on the definability of the majority queries in the continuous framework.

In the pinecone lattice compound Eu2Ir2O7 with Weyl semimetal characteristics, the chirality of the ferromagnetic state plays a crucial role in determining topological properties. Substituting Bi for Eu in Eu2Ir2O7 transforms it from a Weyl semimetal to an electromagnetically induced charge density wave (CDW) compound, making this transition of interest. By inserting Bi at the Eu site, the ferromagnetic state is replaced by an antiferromagnetic state and the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) is significantly altered. A study on the temperature-dependent electrical resistivity of Bi2Ir2O7, through systematic binary substitution in (Eu1-xBix)2Ir2O7, 0 <= x <= 1, indicates the emergence of the CH phase, manifesting as anisotropic and antiferromagnetic charge density wave at 12 K, which breaks the Lorentz symmetry. Analysis of the results suggests that the substitution-induced CH phase, with its electron correlation, is responsible for the modification of the CME and the pinecone structure.

Consider a set-valued mapping whose domain is a closed ball in a Euclidean space and whose range consists of closed, convex subsets of another Euclidean space. The text discusses the existence of a Lipschitz selection for this mapping when it has no zeros, linking this existence to a set-valued mapping from the domain to the range that also has no zeros. We establish existence theorefor Lipschitz selections in two cases: when the set-valued mapping is lower semicontinuous and when its values are compact, providing a new proof for latter scenario.

Consider a random n-tuple $(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ in $\R^d$ that is both cyclic and stationary. A property is attributed to this n-tuple if it remains after applying a random measure $\Phi$ that preserves cyclic symmetry. Our key finding reveals the relationship between the characteristics of this n-tuple and the random variable representing its cumulative sum: $\sum_{i=1}^d X_i$. Specifically, the distribution of this sum must exhibit higher order rejection inequality (HORI) in alignment with the order defined by the $(n-1)$-fold Hilbert lattice. This discovery leads to the conclusion that the characteristics achievable by $\sum_{i=1}^d X_i$ correspond to those attainable through the independent and identically distributed scenario.

Running software systems can be customized through various methods, one of which is runtime configuration. This allows the system to adapt to different environments and users without requiring a new version to be released. Specializing a software system for its intended environment can result in improved response times, smaller download sizes, and reduced resource consumption. However, it remains unclear to what extent this customization also enhances security and reliability.

In this research, we investigate the relationship between software customization and its non-functional properties by examining the effects of runtime configuration on multiple systems and its resulting changes. We evaluate several OzObject systems with differing configurations and investigate how the runtime configuration process affects their security, reliability, performance, and overall functionality.

Our study reveals that runtime configuration can indeed affect a software system's non-functional properties and provides insight into the underlying factors driving these changes. Furthermore, it offers a comprehensive evaluation of several software systems and their behavior when customized, contributing to a clearer understanding of the system being developed.

Light dark matter particles, particularly those weighing less than a GeV, offer an attractive option over heavier, weakly-interacting massive particles. Directly detecting such lightweight particles, however, poses a significant challenge. But if the recoil of a struck nucleus leads to electron ionization, even if the recoil itself is too subtle to be measured, it could still be possible to detect the released electron. This process has been found to significantly boost the sensitivity of direct detection experiments to sub-GeV dark matter. In the present, experiments set global records, and future experiments are likely to reach the cross-sections critical to understanding thermal equilibrium.

This paper proposes a method to produce the most connected pairs of qubit states
via an anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction, resulting in two forms of entangled
states: the Werner state and the singlet state. The initial influence of the
quantum vacuum fluctuation and the balance between this effect and the
anti-spontaneous emission process lead to the production of these entangled
states. The probability amplitudes associated with the anti-Jaynes-Cummings
interaction result in maximum Rabi oscillations and the generation of the Werner
state. Moreover, this process enables the creation of the singlet state through
the interaction with a specific class of isotropic density matrices. The
availability of both Rabi oscillations and the entangled states provides an
efficient pathway to produce the Werner state and the singlet state.

The quality of life and cardiovascular system health are heavily influenced by
correct heart function. Measuring heart rate and variations in inter-beat intervals
can be achieved using the heart-rate variability (HRV) parameter. Precise HRV
estimation is critical for assessing cardiovascular health. Leg movements during
wearable devices' use can introduce noise that hinders accurate HRV
determination, making it challenging to calculate HRV from a standard signal.
This research introduces the Long Short-Term Memory Time Series Transformation
(LSTST) model, which takes leg movement signals and HRV signals as input, then
uses the combined data to predict the HRV value through a series of layered neural
operations, effectively extracting features from both types of signals. The
research also evaluates the performance of the LSTST model with varying input
combinations and compares the results to a baseline model that relies solely on
HRV data. The outcomes indicate the LSTST model's superior accuracy and robustness
when incorporating leg movement signals.

We analyze large deviations of power input by an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle (AOUP) within and outside of a potential well. Using an entropy approach, we derive the rate function for the particle's injected power in various environments. Specifically, we compute the rate function for the particle in open space and also when it's confined to a three-dimensional box. Furthermore, we derive the asymptotic behavior of the rate function as the activity level increases for the case of open space.

This research introduces HUMBI, a large, multi-modal dataset created to study human body language in virtual social interactions. Consisting of over 3000 recordings, the dataset captures text and five body signals — gaze, gesture, posture, and movement — as inputs and outputs. The data involves agents engaging in conversational tasks while the model is to predict their reactions to the text input. Based on the five body signals, the dataset includes four levels of task complexity. The research also presents two baseline tasks and three metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of a body language generation model. Experiments with two existing models and a custom dataset-tuning model on the HUMBI show the dataset to be a reliable testing ground for such tasks. A benchmark model is developed to establish a point of reference for future comparisons and improvements. The dataset is freely available at https://github.com/andrewjgordon/HUMBI.

Despite the growing number of multilingual models, many are task-specific and the advances in one may not greatly benefit another when it comes to language other than English. We address this by proposing a universal approach to transferring neural models across six different languages: French, German, Turkish, Arabic, and Japanese. Our multilingual framework relies on novel transfer functions that allow us to adapt and apply knowledge from a model trained in a non-target language to a new language for a specific task. It involves two key steps: representation transformation to bridge the gap between source and target languages and information fusion to combine the knowledge from the transferred model with the target model. Through comprehensive experiments on a natural language inference task, our framework demonstrates its effectiveness in model transfer and extends model life cycle.

A novel, unsupervised end-to-end video super-resolution (VS-R) method is
proposed, featuring two innovative components: (a) a architecture that
propagates the second-order grid, and (b) a deformable alignment technique
guided by the flow guidance. The proposed approach overcomes a fundamental
challenge in VS-R, which is aligning low-resolution (LR) frames with high
resolution (HR) training frames for implicit ground truth. The proposed model
incorporates both contributions to enhance performance, as demonstrated by
comprehensive evaluations in terms of efficiency and visual quality on various
images and videos.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can significantly
benefit a knowledge-aware model when it is exposed to analogous tasks.
Conversely, this model may suffer performance degradation when faced with
unanticipated tasks. An existing method attempts to mitigate this issue by using
a self-training approach based on semi-supervised learning principles. Yet, it
still relies heavily on prior knowledge and does not fully exploit the latent
structure within shared representations. This paper proposes a novel method to
overcome this limitation by training a shared representation that is informed by
the intrinsic task latent structure, discovered through a task latent structure
induction module employing a Bayesian change detection algorithm. Furthermore,
an intrinsic Bayesian change detection is applied to the task actions within the
shared representation to facilitate multi-task learning through self-training. The
proposed method is evaluated on a range of 16-benchmark datasets comprising
multiple tasks, which reveal its superiority over existing baselines when tasks
are related and its resilience to unseen tasks.

We have improved the performance of heat engines experiencing a finite time by identifying the most efficient protocols under specific conditions. These optimal protocols feature a constant product of bath temperature and the cube of a key stiffness factor, which factor remains consistent across all values of the stiffness, representing the system's slow and fast movements. This discovery reflects the trade-off between the system's slow and fast components, leading to a non-adiabatic but thermally balanced outcome.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm tracks based on historical data and corresponding storm intensities. To model the effects of rising storm waters, the research employs a simplified surge approximation and identifies vulnerable areas using a grid-based model. This method estimates the probability of rising water levels at power substations to assess the risk of power loss. In addition, the post-hurricane recovery process is addressed by generating an efficient and rapid restoration plan utilizing an integer programming model. This model takes into account the availability of repair crews and the minimization of power restoration time. An illustrative case demonstrating the model's effectiveness and scalability is provided using the power loss and cost outcomes on the Reliability Assessment Model for Electric Infrastructure (RAMIE) system in Florida.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

We define a family of 2D baker map variants that exhibit chaotic behavior with zero measure, expanding in the opposite direction to the standard baker map. We develop a comprehensive mathematical framework to accurately represent the dynamics and create a precise model for this system, analogous to the well-known Lorez attractor. Additionally, we generate corresponding Lypovov Larkin experiments, similar to the famous Benoit Mandelbrot portrait.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex model featuring additional particles. A critical method for resolving this query involves scrutinizing extended scalar models using future high-energy collider facilities, including the potential proton-proton collider with 27 and 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, and advanced lepton colliders at 3 and 1000 GeV.

This paper presents a novel neural network architecture, where the pitch
dependent dilated convolution layers are used as a method for audio PITCH
dependent audio PITCH dependent audio PITCH dependent audio pitch dependent
audio waveform generation. The proposed approach, where multiple neural
networks are used to model audio conditioned on pitch, demonstrates improved
generative capabilities and allows for novel applications in audio processing.

Recommender Systems have become increasingly popular due to the data explosion and associated information overload. Among various approaches, Collaborative Filtering remains the most prominent and successful technique. However, its effectiveness is hindered by several challenges such as the cold-start and sparsity issues. To tackle these limitations, hybrid models have been proposed, blending different methods to improve prediction accuracy. In this research, a new neural network-based model is introduced, designed to learn implicit user-item interactions space and accurately predict missing ratings for user-item interactions. The model is further enhanced by incorporating a residual connection, resulting in the proposed User-Item Residual Neural Network (URIN). Experimental evaluations on two standard benchmark datasets demonstrate the proposed method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art recommendation systems in terms of prediction accuracy and generalization ability.

Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of the Sun, selecting lines based on their relevance to Earth-analogue detections, and measured their variability during active periods using solar data and forecasts. We employed a classifier to automatically distinguish these periods and used the information to analyze these lines' variability. We found that active regions on the Sun cause significant variability in the spectral features, even in quiet stars, and identified lines that effectively reflect a star's magnetic behavior, and recommend their use as additional stellar activity indicators.

To differentiate between different theoretical predictions about tunneling from topological surface states to a topological superconductor, we need to examine how tunneling conductance changes under various conditions. Our focus is on understanding the distinct behaviors of tunneling conductance at low and high voltages as temperature and bias vary. We present and compare three different tunneling models, each with its own underlying assumptions. Firstly, we look at a scenario where tunneling occurs without resistance, we then compare this to a model where tunneling conductance is limited by resistance, and finally, we explore a model where inelastic tunneling plays a significant role. A key distinction we find is that the temperature-dependent broadening of the Majorana peak at low voltages is common to all three models. However, the behavior at higher voltages is where significant differences emerge, with the model including resistance showing a conductance peak that grows with voltage, whereas the models without resistance or with inelastic tunneling show conductance peaks that decrease with increasing voltage.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Image editing or enhancement tasks like color correction, image restoration, and aesthetic evaluation often do not have a single definitive solution due to the vast amount of possible outcomes. To bridge the gap between human expertise and machine learning, previous approaches have relied on user input in the form of color adjustment tools or style transfer from reference images. However, these methods can be cumbersome and produce results that require manual fine-tuning by eye.

To address these limitations, our fully-automated system generates a diverse range of high-quality images to assist human users in generating data-driven editing guidelines. Our approach combines a novel variational autoencoder with a new scoring mechanism to produce a set of styles from low-dimensional data. Our system produces results that preserve the original image's content while producing a variety of visually appealing and artistically styled outputs. Our method represents a significant advancement in the domain of image editing and assistance, as it automates the image generation and guideline creation process more effectively than previous methods.

This technical report showcases the winning model of the AudioVisLab task at the Signal Processing and Analysis for Video Understanding challenge, a 2021 online machine learning competition targeting multi-modal video understanding in a horizontal context. We develop an video representation that integrates textual and visual information, utilizing outcome-agnostic text feature extraction from video frames combined with deep learning-based video encoding. To leverage this representation, we employ sophisticated aggregation techniques and combine it with keypoint-based attention over visual features. The ultimate model strategy involves ensembling multiple models with different hyperparameters and late fusion of audio and text branches, incorporating domain-specific text pre-training. We achieve a mean averaged recall score of 0.4313 on the test set, securing first place among 166 participants in the competition. This report provides an exhaustive description of our approach, including discussion of potential limitations and future research directions.

This field research focused on snow deposition in turbulent airflow. Researchers combined numerical simulations of snowflake dynamics within a turbulent flow dataset, a laboratory experiment to capture vacuum-deposited snowflake patterns, and a new approach to obtain high-resolution measurements of snow deposition in real-time. Snowflakes in the simulated and experimental setups exhibited consistent sizes and rotated as they settled, particularly aligning with the spiral vortex features in the flow, where concentrated concentrations formed along their vortex core and arms. In the turbulent flow, snowflake settling velocities were 10-20% lower than their terminal setting velocities, while in the pipe flow, their terminal setting velocities were mostly observed. Comparative analysis of the simulated vacuum-deposited patterns and the measured snow deposition patterns showed a significant match, with both displaying concentrated concentrations in the vortex structure, with the most intense concentrations at the innermost area on the vortex, where turbulent kinetic energy dissipation is the highest.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an effective tool for creating internal representations of the external environment, based on the concept that the brain must minimize the difference between what it expects and what it actually experiences through either updating its internal understanding or changing its interactions with the external environment. This document presents a neural network design that can implement the core mechanism of active inference, utilizing our previously developed framework for predictive coding and our creation of specialized neural structures that facilitate complex mathematical calculations. The proposed design matches the architecture of the human brain's prefrontal cortex and temporal lobe, employing a top-down mechanism where the larger lobe's neural outputs match its greater number of neurons to influence the smaller lobe's understanding, thereby rectifying any discrepancies in predictions through both updating and action.

In experimental facilities such as high energy physics and cosmology, the amount of data generated in real-time often exceeds the capacity to be stored. This data overload poses significant challenges in real-time data analysis and feedback management. To address these issues, the ability to process data in real-time on the operator interface is essential. We have developed a system for real-time data visualization and interaction that can handle both single-event data and aggregated data streams. This system is implemented in the ClickGUI environment, which is used in conjunction with the Frontier CLI system to provide a comprehensive data management solution.

Utilizing Finzi's gravity theory that enhances interactions at large scales, we analyze galaxy clusters from a thermodynamic perspective, establishing a model that generalizes the Flory theory's free energy expression, now applicable to a broader gravity context. We extend this model by developing a new stochastic dynamics, for both the particle-level Dinelli process and the system's thermodynamic behavior, then compare clustering effects across various gravity models, including those of the form $1/r^\alpha$, with the standard Newtonian $1/r^2$ framework, demonstrating that Finzi's model predicts increased clustering at large scales, akin to the effect of an attractive force, without violating thermodynamic principles.

A type of convex geometric hypergraph, known as cgh, comprises a set of subsets originating from strictly convex point sets in the plane. In this study, researchers explore a specific type of problem associated with cghs, referred to as removal type problems. These involve determining the maximum number of edges in cghs that can be created using n vertices while ensuring none contain specified types of 'forbidden' configurations. Using this approach, several significant results are presented that provide novel proof for existing results and address open issues related to specific types of removal style problems.

To gain a better understanding of the relative contributions of different processes, the angular distributions and energy spectra of $\alpha$ particles produced via the $^{12}$C(d,p)$^{13}$C,$^{13}$C$^{*}$ decay, $^{13}$N$\beta^{+}$ decay and ($^{13}$N,p)$^{12}$C processes have been measured up to 35.3 cm$^{3}$ from the reaction center, with the aim of distinguishing their signals. The measurements were taken at energies of 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 30, 40, and 50 keV, with angular separations of up to 120 degrees. The energy contributions of the three processes have been determined using non-negative least squares fitting and the relative contributions of the ($^{13}$N,p)$^{12}$C process compared to the sum of the other two processes have also been calculated. When comparing the simulated energy and angular distributions of the ($^{13}$N,p)$^{12}$C process with the experimental results, using the G4IonEmStandard option in the Geant4 simulation, a significant discrepancy was found. However, using the simplified energy and angular distributions provided by the NUBIBRIDE database for the angular integration led to excellent

A previously overlooked ability in biological climbing is the peak vertical stride displacement, where the climber's stride peaks when it is equal to its body length. A dynamic model was developed to explain the peak vertical stride displacement, where a balance of inertial force and gravitational force leads to a peak in this phenomenon. A biomimetic robot named Trident, which mimics the movement of California chain salamanders and the movement of lampreys, was designed using a peak vertical stride-displacement-invariant control strategy. This robot achieved peak vertical stride displacements of 1.36, 1.27, and 0.88 times its body length while climbing on 2D surfaces with 30, 25, and 15 degrees of inclination, respectively. Moreover, the Tronder model demonstrated peak vertical stride displacement, resulting in its successful simplification and increased stride frequency, which led to its stable performance. This research shows the potential of peak vertical stride displacement as a universal characteristic of climbing motion, which could inspire biomimetic climbing robots for use in rescue missions and space exploration.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrate that target-reaching strategies outperform those focused on reducing initial tumor size.

Wireless devices in close proximity can transmit through the air using Device-to-device (D2D) technology, enabling faster and more efficient data transfer, similar to the exchange of images, videos, and backups of personal files, which we experience in everyday lives. A critical challenge lies in optimizing D2D scheduling to balance load and maximize throughput. Research has focused on two key aspects of this problem: minimizing makespan and reducing total completion time. A common approach to addressing these objectives is to reduce the weighted flow time of jobs, allowing us to develop efficient algorithms. A novel algorithm, WFDTS, is proposed to yield an O(1/n) approximation for weighted flow time, improving upon existing solutions with O(log n) or O(1/log n) approximations in specific job release scenarios. Additionally, WFDTS outperforms the top existing results by achieving better performance while offering a simplified approach.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity. This review covers the applications of helicity in various aspects of flow dynamics, including its role in the generation of magnetic fields, its implications in the decay of turbulent flows and its behavior in rotating systems. It also provides an account of recent research developments in helicity theory, its evolution and the problems that were addressed within the framework of inviscid fluids.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in a previous paper by Berry and Keating by examining large complex geometric optics on a compact manifold with a specific property. They identified both the left and right reflection coefficients along with their respective asymptotic behaviors as a specific parameter increases. Additionally, they demonstrated how to use these coefficients to reconstruct a class of potential functions through an inverse scattering problem. Notably, the authors showed that solutions to this inverse scattering problem can be found even when limited to only the reflection data, without requiring additional scattering information. The authors also highlighted the uniqueness of the potential function within its respective class during the process of reconstruction.

Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of merging compact binary systems,
including the gravitational waves they emit, have been modeled to late post-Newtonian
order $5 \Omega$. This allows for the determination of how the orbital frequency,
spin orientations, and final eccentricities of the binary system evolve. For
binary systems composed of non-spinning compact objects with specific mass
configurations, it has been found that their orbital eccentricities after the
orbital recoil velocity peaks is approximately $e(f_{\rm orb}=162\,\rm Hz)\simeq
0.116-0.083$. Furthermore, for spinning binaries that merge nearly head-on, it has
been observed that the binary's total spin tends to rotate in the direction of its
angular momentum, and that orbital eccentricity modes can induce spin rotation in
the orbital plane. These predictions align reasonably with numerical relativity
simulations and post-Newtonian theory regarding how binary systems' orbital
eccentricities and spin dynamics evolve.

A widely used method to enhance the efficiency of free-electron lasers is called self-amplitude modulation (SAM). In our research, we have developed a computational model for simulating self-insertion of free-electron laser pulses into the relativistic chirp of the electron beam. Our model takes into account the full energy spread of the electron beam, which differs from previous two-dimensional models. Our findings demonstrate that efficient self-amplitude modulation is possible across the entire pulse and are compatible with current Free-Electron Laser experiments. However, we have identified an imbalance in SAM amplification when using long wavelengths or high energy spread. In such cases, the pulse's leading edge experiences over-amplification, while the trailing edge remains under-amplified.

Event detection on dynamic graphs holds significant value across various fields, yet it faces challenges due to inherent issues like entity entity associations in the graph and temporal changes from sequential subgraph extraction. To overcome these obstacles, we developed a novel approach called DynED, which integrates an attention-based temporal graph neural network with self-supervised learning. The proposed model employs event-driven representation learning to ensure consistent entity representations and maintains subgraph diversity. Additionally, we created a new benchmark dataset and conducted comprehensive evaluations of dynamic graph representations. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of DynED in event detection and graph representation. The code and dataset of our model are accessible at https://github.com/zhengqianlee/DynED.

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent.
